en: The Glorious *Hevajra*, the Great King of Tantras,
Part I. Chapter One.
Oṃ, homage to the glorious Hevajra!
Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling within the bhagas of the Vajra Ladies, who are the heart of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas.

There, the Blessed One said: "The heart of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas is the Lord, more secret than the secret. Oh, Vajragarbha, well done, well done! O Great Compassionate One, Great Bodhisattva—listen to the heart of the Bodhisattva Vajrasattva, the Mahāsattva, the Samayasattva, and the Jñānasattva, which is known by the name Hevajra.
Vajragarbha said:
Why does one become Vajrasattva? How does one become Mahāsattva? By what does one become Samayasattva? May the Blessed One explain this to me. (3) The Blessed One replied:
The indestructible is called "vajra," and the being (*sattva*) is the unity of the three realms of existence.
Through this wisdom and this reasoning, he is known as Vajrasattva.
(4) Filled with the essence of great gnosis, he is called Mahāsattva.
Because he is constantly engaged in the commitments (*samaya*), he is called a *samayasattva*.
(5) [In summary, by means of the practice of awakening, he is designated a *bodhisattva*.]
“Through the union of wisdom and gnosis, the Gnosis-being is the Tathāgata.
Vajragarbha said: “By what means does Hevajra possess such a compendium of names?”
"What is signified by the syllable *he*, and likewise, what is said by *vajra*?
The Blessed One replied:
"By *he* is meant great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and *vajra* is said to be wisdom (*prajñā*)."
Listen as I proclaim to you that tantra which consists of wisdom and skillful means.
The wise know its many kinds of powers: the great ritual display of summoning by sight, as well as paralyzing, expelling, the immobilization of armies, and malevolent magic. (7–8)
The cause of the arising and abiding of the yoginīs according to the rule,
their capacity, their knowledge and realization, and the manner in which the deities arise—
first of all, there is one cause for the arising of Heruka.
O Vajragarbha of great compassion, beings are liberated by means of existence itself. (10) They are bound by the bond of existence and liberated through the thorough knowledge of it.
A wise person should regard existence as that which is to be cultivated, and non-existence through thorough knowledge.
In that same way, one should meditate upon Śrī Heruka through the thorough knowledge of non-existence.
This great gnosis residing within the body is free from all conceptual constructions;
though it pervades all things and resides in the body, it is not born of the body. (11–12)
Vajragarbha said:
"O Bhagavān, in the vajra-body, which are the channels?"

The Blessed One said: "There are thirty-two channels. Thirty-two carry the bodhicitta and flow into the place of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). Among them, three channels are primary: lalanā, rasanā, and avadhūtī.
Lalanā has the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*), while rasanā is established as method (*upāya*)."
The *avadhūtī* is in the middle region, free from the grasped and the grasper.
(14) Lalanā carries Akṣobhya and Rasanā carries blood; that which is proclaimed as carrying the moon of wisdom is celebrated as the *avadhūtī*. (15)
Abhedyā, Sūkṣmarūpā, Divyā, Vāmā, Vāminī, Kūrmajā, Bhāvakī, Sekā, Doṣā, Viṣṭā, Mātarī,
Śavarī, Śītadā, Oṣmā, Lalanā, Avadhūtī, and Rasanā. (16)
Pravaṇā, Kṛṣṇavarṇā, Surūpiṇī, Sāmānyā, Hetudāyikā;
(17) Viyogā, Premaṇī, Siddhā, Pāvakī, Sumanas, Traivṛttā, Kāminī, Gehā, Caṇḍikā, and Māradārikā. (18)
Vajragarbha said:
"Bhagavān, what are these thirty-two channels like?
The Bhagavān replied: (19)
All [phenomena] are transformations of the three realms of existence, devoid of the grasped and the grasper;
alternatively, they are conceptualized as the characteristics of entities by every means.

(20) The classification of the vows (*saṃvara*) is also explained: *Āli* and *Kāli*, moon and sun, wisdom and method, the Dharma-body, Enjoyment-body, Emanation-body, Great Bliss, body, speech, and mind—thus it was by me. (21)

By the syllable *e* is Locanā-devī; by the syllable *vaṃ*, Māmakī is remembered. By the syllable *ma*, Pāṇḍarā; and by the syllable *yā*, Tāraṇī is remembered. (22) In the nirmāṇacakra, there is a lotus with sixty-four petals.
The wheel of dharma has eight petals;
the wheel of enjoyment has sixteen petals;
the wheel of great bliss has thirty-two petals.
The arrangement according to the sequence of the number of wheels consists of four moments:
namely, the variegated (*vicitra*), the ripening (*vipāka*), the crushing (*vimarda*), and the signless (*vilakṣaṇa*).
There are four limbs:
service, close service, accomplishment, and great accomplishment; these are the four noble truths.
And suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—these are the four truths. Furthermore, there are the four realities:
the reality of the self, the reality of mantra, the reality of the deity, and the reality of gnosis.
There are four joys:
joy (*ānanda*), supreme joy (*paramānanda*), the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*), and innate joy (*sahajānanda*).
There are four schools (*nikāya*).
Sthāvarī, Sarvāstivāda, Saṃvidī, and Mahāsaṅghī.
(29) Moon and sun, *āli* and *kāli*, the sixteen transits (*saṃkrānti*), the sixty-four *daṇḍas*, the thirty-two *nāḍīs*, and the four watches (*prahāra*)—thus all are fourfold.
(30) Caṇḍālī blazes at the navel.
It burns the five Tathāgatas.
And it burns the eyes and so forth.
When burnt, I flow forth as the moon.
(31) This is the first chapter, on the Family of Hevajra of the Body, Speech, and Mind of all Tathāgatas.
Part I, Chapter II.
We shall explain the chapter on mantras.
The mantra for the bali offering to all elemental spirits is:
Oṃ, the letter A is the mouth of all phenomena because they are unarisen from the beginning; Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā. (1)
The seed-syllables of the Tathāgatas: BŪṂ AṂ JRĪṂ KHAṂ HŪṂ. (2) The heart-mantra of Hevajra.
Oṃ deva picu vajra hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. (3) These are all mantra-words:
beginning with the syllable Oṃ and ending with Svāhā, they are interspersed with the syllables Hūṃ and Phaṭ. (4)
The mantra for agitating the city:
Oṃ a ka ca ṭa ta pa ya śa svāhā. (5) The seed-syllable of the Yoginīs.
a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au aṃ aḥ (6) [are the seed-syllables] of the two-armed [form].
Oṃ trailokyākṣepa hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā (7).
For the four-armed [deity]: Oṃ jvala jvala abhyo hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. (8) For the six-armed [deity].
Oṃ kiṭi kiṭi vajra hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. (9) This is the mantra for the blessing of body, speech, and mind. Oṃ āḥ hūṃ. (10)
The mantra for purifying the ground:
Oṃ rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. (11) This is for immobilization.
Oṃ hūṃ svāhā (12) for subjugation. Oṃ aṃ svāhā (13).
Uccāṭana: Oṃ Khaṃ Svāhā (14).
Vidveṣaṇa.
Oṃ jrīṃ svāhā. (15) [This is] for the purpose of malevolent magic. Oṃ buṃ svāhā. (16)
Attraction: Oṃ hūṃ svāhā. (17) Killing.
Oṃ ghuḥ svāhā. (18) Oṃ kurukulle hrīḥ svāhā. (19)

Having fashioned an image of Ananta with the syllables Oṃ Āḥ Phuḥ, one should bathe it with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta). One should worship it with black flowers and smear it with the juice of the *nāgadamaraka* plant. One should smear its head with elephant ichor (*hastimada*).

Having enclosed it within two joined shallow bowls (*śarāva*), one should place it there and fill it with the milk of a black cow. One should wrap it with a thread spun by a black maiden. Having constructed a lotus pond in the northwestern direction, one should install that Ananta there. On its bank, one should draw a maṇḍala.

One should prepare the colored powders as follows: black powder from charcoal from a cremation ground; white powder from powdered human bone; yellow powder from orpiment; red powder from bricks from a cremation ground; green powder from *caurya* leaves and powdered human bone; and blue powder from powdered human bone and charcoal from a cremation ground. Having fashioned the mandala with these powders and having marked it out with a cord from a cremation ground, one should draw a three-cubit mandala measuring three thumb-breadths and so forth, and in its center, one should paint Hevajra treading upon Ananta.

[The practitioner should visualize the deity] with eight faces, four feet, adorned with sixteen arms, and possessing twenty-four eyes and so forth. Thereafter, in a secluded place, the preceptor, with an inwardly fierce mind, should recite the mantra:
*Oṃ ghuru ghuru ghuḍu ghuḍu masa masa ghaṭa ghaṭa ghoṭaya ghoṭaya anantakṣobhakarāya nāgādhipataye he he ru ru ka*.
Draw forth, draw forth the nāgas dwelling in the seven underworlds! Rain down, rain down! Roar, roar!
Phuḥ phuḥ phuḥ phuḥ phuḥ phuḥ phuḥ phuḥ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!

If they do not rain, then one should recite this mantra in reverse; [then] they will rain. If they still do not rain, then their heads shall burst like the flower-cluster of an arjaka tree. This is the procedure for the rainy season. (20) I shall now describe the dispersal of clouds.
Sitting upon a cloth from a cemetery, one should disperse them by means of mantra-recitation.
Oṃ āryaśmaśānapriyāya hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the procedure for dispersing clouds.
(21) I shall now describe the ritual for preparing chalk in order to destroy enemy armies.
Having ground chalk together with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and *kuṭhāracchinnā*, one should prepare a wick (*vati*).
The mantra is: OṂ VAJRAKARTARI HEVAJRĀYA HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ.

For the sake of accomplishment, one should recite [the mantra] ten million times; for the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*), one hundred thousand times. One should wrap that [substance] around the neck of the vessel used for the rite to be accomplished (*sādhyakarma*). Having wrapped it, one should break it; all enemies become headless. This is the ritual of the Vajra-Saw (*vajrakartari-vidhi*). (22) By one desiring to split the gods, a sectarian mark (*tilaka*) must be prepared. One should grind the seed of Brahmā (*brahmabīja*), consecrated under the Puṣya asterism and mixed with what is cut by an axe, during a solar eclipse, using Akṣobhya. Having ground it, one should consecrate an axe. Treading upon it with the foot, one should recite the mantra.

Oṃ vajrakuṭhāra pāṭaya 2 hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Having recited this ten million times, one should apply it as a tilaka; whatever it touches shall burst open. This is the ritual for splitting deities. (23)

One who desires to cause a blazing conflagration should write the name of the enemy on a leaf of the *arka* plant with a paste made from poison, *rājikā*, *aravana*, and *citraka*. One should cast it into a fire of chaff and recite the mantra ten thousand times:
*oṃ hevajra jvala 2 śatrūn bhrūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Success is achieved through ten thousand recitations.

(24) One who wishes to cause vomiting of liquor should visualize the syllable *maṃ* at the navel of the person to be acted upon. One should visualize a belly full of liquor produced from the syllable *maṃ*. He is seen to vomit, and he disgorges the liquor.

(25) One who wishes to bring a woman under one's power should go to the foot of an *aśoka* tree on the eighth day of the month of *aśoka*, put on red garments, and eat *madana* fruit. Having applied a forehead mark (*tilaka*) with the juice of *kāmācikā*, one should worship and recite the mantra.
Oṃ hrīḥ, may [Name] be brought under my control, svāhā!
By reciting this ten thousand times, she comes.
(26) One who desires to bring the moon and sun under control should fashion images of the moon and sun out of rice flour and cast them into adamantine water (vajrodaka), while reciting the mantra.

Oṃ candrārka mācala mācala tiṣṭha tiṣṭha hevajrāya hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. One should recite this seven crores of times. It remains; the moon and sun become indistinguishable by night or day. This is the procedure for the stabilization of the moon and sun. (27)

With this mantra, *oṃ nagrā nagrā*, at the time of twilight, for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose, a maiden should consecrate her eyes one hundred and eight times; having worshipped with the fivefold offerings of flowers, incense, and lamps, she should then invite [the deity]. On the fourteenth or the eighth day, at the break of dawn, having established a water-pot and other requisites, she should consecrate oil and lac-dye one hundred and eight times with this very same mantra.

Afterwards, having smeared the practitioner’s thumb with consecrated lac-juice and washed it with oil, he should show it to a young girl and say, "Tell me, by whom has my property been stolen? Thereupon, she will say, "By so-and-so. This is the procedure for searching for lost property according to Vajrajyotiṣa.
(28) When "Oṃ veḍuyā veḍuyā" is uttered, the elephant flees.
(29) When "Oṃ marmā marmā" is uttered, the tiger flees. (30)
When "oṃ teliyā teliyā" is uttered, the *gaṇḍa* flees.
(31) When "ili mili phuḥ phuḥ" is uttered, the serpent flees.
(32) One should show one's hand with the hand of Dhanapālavaineya; the dog flees. (33)
Vajrā, Gaurī, Vārī, Vajraḍākī, and Nairātmikā—
through the yoga of Bhūcarī and Khecarī, the practitioner performs rites such as paralyzing and so forth.
(34) The second chapter, on Mantras.
Part I. Chapter III. We shall now explain the chapter on the deities (*devatāpaṭalam*).
First, one should cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*); likewise, in the second [stage], compassion (*karuṇā*).
In the third [meditation], one should cultivate joy; finally, one should cultivate equanimity toward all.
Therefore, once again—
First is the realization of emptiness, second is the gathering of the seed-syllable,
third is the accomplishment of the image, and fourth is the placement of the syllable.
(2) Having first visualized the sun by means of the syllable *repha* [before oneself]...
At that navel, there is a double-vajra born from the syllable *hūṃ*;
with that very vajra, one should visualize a wall and the binding of a cage. (3)
First, the wise one should meditate on the corpse as being of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*; the yogin, standing upon it, should visualize himself as Heruka. Then... (4) From that...
One should visualize the syllable *repha* in one’s own heart, from which arises a solar disc;
in that very place, one should also visualize the syllable *hūṃ*, whose nature is wisdom and means—black in color, most formidable, and born from the *vajra*. (5)
One should visualize the reality-syllable *HŪṂ* situated in the center of the vajra-navel.
Again, having seen it transformed from the syllable *HŪṂ*, one should visualize it as the essence of hatred.
One should indeed meditate with devotion upon Vajrajanma Mahākṛṣṇa, who resembles a blue lotus, or who has the luster of dark-blue and red;
having beheld the Lord Vajrajanma Mahākṛpa in the sky. (7)
One should worship [the deity] with the eight goddesses, who wear all types of ornaments:
Caurī, who holds a deer-marked [moon]; Gaurī, who holds a vessel for the sun;
Vetālī, whose hand holds water; and Ghasmarī, who holds medicinal herbs. (8–9)
Pukkasī holds a vajra in her hand, and Śavarī likewise holds a vessel of nectar;
Caṇḍālī plays the hand-drum (ḍamaru). By these [goddesses] the Lord is worshipped, his neck embraced by Ḍombī, he who is impassioned with great passion. (10)
The seed-syllable consisting of the moon (*ca*), the line (*ndrāli*), and the sun (*kālimārtaṇḍa*) shall be situated in the center.
They say that this alone is *sattva*, whose intrinsic nature is supreme bliss.
It radiates forth from its own body, pervading the entire expanse of the sky.
The yogin should bring those who are to be subdued into his heart and become one whose nature is aversion.
He has a complexion of dark red, with eyes like the blooming bandhūka flower;
his hair is tawny and stands upright in curls, and he is adorned with the five mudrās. (12–13)
The wheel, the earring, the necklace, the bracelet on the hand, and the girdle—
these mudrās are proclaimed as the purity of the five Buddhas. (14) With a wrathful gaze, clad in a tiger skin, he has the appearance of a sixteen-year-old.
In the left [hand] is a vajra-skull cup, and also a khaṭvāṅga staff to the left;
in the right is a black vajra, consisting of the utterance of the syllable HŪṂ. (15)

The Lord sports in the charnel ground, surrounded by the eight yoginīs; it is designated as "charnel ground" by way of this principle of "breathing. (16) He has four arms due to the purity of having conquered the four Māras. Possessing the color and form previously described, he arises from the syllable *HŪṂ*. In his first left arm is a human skull-cup filled with the blood of gods and asuras; in his first right arm is a vajra. With the remaining two arms, he embraces the Prajñā. Vajravārāhī, the Prajñā, has the same form as the Blessed One. (17)

He has six arms and three faces; the left is red, the right has the luster of the moon, and the first [face] is blue. He is naked, possessing the color and form previously described. The six arms represent the purity of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). In the first left arm is a trident, in the first right arm a vajra, in the second left arm a bell, and in the second right arm a flaying knife (*kartī*). With the remaining two arms he embraces the Vajra-Chain (*vajraśṛṅkhalā*). Just as the Blessed One is, so too is Prajñā; in her right and left hands she holds a flaying knife and a skull-cup (*kapāla*). He stands treading upon a corpse that embodies the three realms. (18)
The third chapter: The Deities of Hevajra, the Body, Speech, and Mind of all Tathāgatas.
Part I, Chapter IV.
We shall now explain the chapter on the consecration of the deities (*devatābhiṣeka*).

Having emitted a ray of light from the seed-syllable within one’s own heart, which has the brilliance of black [light] and the form of a hook, one draws forth the Buddhas residing in the three realms; having worshipped them with the eight Mothers, one causes them to enter. (1)
"Oṃ, may all the Tathāgatas consecrate me!

Thus, by those Buddhas in the form of Heruka, he is consecrated with five vases filled with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), which are the very essence of the five Tathāgatas. While he is being consecrated, a rain of flowers falls, the sound of drums resounds, and a rain of saffron (*kuṅkuma*) occurs. 82)

He is fully honored by Rūpavajrā and the others; the Vajra-songs are sung by Locanā and the others. While being consecrated, the Lord of one's own family resides upon the crown of the head. By this means, Heruka is perfected; having meditated upon the visualization of the empowerment at the three junctions of the day, one should arise and remain in the form of the deity.
The Fourth Chapter: The Empowerment.
Part I. Chapter V.
Now we shall explain the chapter on reality (tattvapaṭala) according to its own nature.
There is no form and no seer; no sound and no hearer; no smell and no smeller; no taste and no taster;
no touch and no toucher; nor is there mind or mental factors. (1)
The knower of yoga should always honor his mother and sister,
as well as the dancer, the washerwoman, the Vajra woman, the Caṇḍālī, and the Brāhmaṇī.
One who is devoted to reality should perform worship according to the method of wisdom and skillful means.
(2) One should serve [the teacher] with great effort so that no separation occurs;
for if one is unprotected, suffering is caused by beasts of prey, thieves, fire, and earth-dwellers. (3)
The mudrās are said to be the five families for the sake of liberation.
Because one is sealed by means of this [vajra], it is therefore called a "mudrā.
[These are] Vajra, Padma, Karma, Tathāgata, and Ratna.
O Great Compassionate One, they say there are five types of families that are supreme:
in the Vajra [family], the ḍombī shall be the mudrā; likewise, in the Padma [family], the nartī; in the Karma [family], the rajakī is declared; and in the Tathāgata [family], the brāhmaṇī. (5–6)
In the Jewel [family], Caṇḍālinī is to be known; these are determined as the five mudrās.
This is briefly described as the Tathāgata family.
The glorious one has gone to suchness and likewise returned from it.
By means of this wisdom and through this reasoning, the Tathāgata is thus designated. (8) They say that families are of six kinds, but in brief they are fivefold;
subsequently, they become threefold through the division of body, speech, and mind. (9)
The five families consist of the five elements, which have the nature of the five aggregates. That by which one is reckoned or counted is called a "family" (*kula*).
There is no practitioner, there is no state of being, there is no mantra, and there is no deity.
The mantra and the deity abide as being of the nature of the non-proliferated (*niṣprapañca*).
Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Amogha, Ratna, Āroli, Sātvika, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Sarva—the Awakened One is called the Reality (*tattva*). (11–12)

He is Brahmā because of his being extinguished (*nirvṛti*); he is called Buddha because of awakening (*buddha*); Viṣṇu because of pervading (*viṣaṇa*); Śiva because of eternal auspiciousness; Sarva because he abides in the self of all.
And he is Tattva because of true bliss, and Vibuddha because of the awakening to delight.
Because it arises within the body, it is called "deity" (*devatā*).
One who possesses *bhaga* is called "Bhagavān" by the Buddha;
they say that *bhaga* consists of the sixfold qualities, such as sovereignty and the rest.
Alternatively, he is called Bhagavān because he shatters the Māras, beginning with the afflictions (*kleśa*).
(15) Wisdom (*prajñā*) is called the "mother" because she gives birth to the world; likewise, wisdom is called the "sister" insofar as she demonstrates differentiation (*vibhāga*). (16)
She is proclaimed as both a washerwoman and a dancer;
she is likewise remembered as a "washerman's daughter" because she colors all sentient beings.
And because she milks out virtue, she is called the "daughter."
O Great Compassionate One, wisdom is called the dancer because of its flickering nature; since the Blessed Lady is intangible, she is therefore proclaimed as the Dombī. (18)
Recitation (*japa*) is said to be the continuous utterance of vowels and consonants;
the mandala is the footprint, for it is called a mandala because of its being ground down (*malana*).
The snapping of the hands is the mudrā, as is likewise the pressing of the fingers. (19)

That which is contemplated is the object of meditation, and that from which contemplation arises is also the object of meditation. (20) The happiness obtained from one's father is experienced by oneself;
that happiness by which death is met is called the bliss of meditative absorption. (21)
The fifth chapter on reality.
Part I, Chapter VI.
Hereafter I shall explain the supreme conduct that has reached the further shore, by which one proceeds to the Siddhānta through the cause of accomplishment in Hevajra. (1)
The practitioner should wear divine earrings on his ears;
a discus should be worn on the head, and two bracelets on the hands.
A girdle should likewise be worn at the waist, and anklets on the feet.
An armlet on the base of the upper arm and a necklace of bones around the neck;
a tiger skin for clothing and the consumption of the five nectars— such is the conduct of a person in the yoga of Heruka among the five colors.
That which is endowed with five colors is conceived as a single color,
because no distinction is perceived between the many and the single color.
(5) Meditation on the beautiful is taught [to be performed] either upon a single tree or in a cemetery.
Likewise, in a delightful mother’s house, or else in a secluded wilderness;
when some warmth has arisen, if one desires to practice the conduct, and if there is a wish to attain accomplishment, one should practice by means of this conduct. (6–7)

Taking this Vajra-maiden— who has a beautiful face and wide eyes, who is adorned with beauty and youth, whose limbs are dark as the blue lotus, who has been consecrated by herself, and who is compassionate— one awakens to perform the conduct. (8)
In the absence of the Vajra family, she should be taken according to the family of one’s own chosen deity;
or else, one should take her who has arisen from another family and been consecrated by the deposition of the seed-syllable of enlightenment. (9)
If song is sung out of bliss, then it is supreme and endowed with the vajra;
if one dances when bliss has arisen for the sake of liberation, then the concentrated yogi should perform the dance in the state of the vajra. (10)
Akṣobhya is in the form of the wheel, Amitābha is the nature of the earring;
Ratneśa is on the necklace, and Vairocana is said to be in the hand. Amoghasiddhi resides in the girdle, and Prajñā has the form of the khaṭvāṅga staff.
Through the purification of hatred, the yogin [manifests] in the form of the hand-drum (*ḍamaru*) and the skull-bowl (*kapāla*).
By means of the purification of the mantra, singing, dancing, and meditative cultivation are said to be established.
Therefore, the yogin should always and constantly perform song and dance. (13) One should eat medicine and drink water regularly;
thus, old age and death shall not afflict him, and he shall always be protected. (14)
There, one born from the syllable *hūṃ* should join a crown made of stolen hair;
according to the practice of yoga, one should wear the skull-bowls of the five Buddhas.
Having fashioned fragments of skull-bones five finger-widths long, they are always worn upon the crown.
The glass rosary is double-stranded by virtue of the nature of wisdom and means;
the yogin wears the sacred thread made of ashes and hair as his conduct.
(16) Recitation is the sound of the hand-drum, and meditation is the wisdom-khaṭvāṅga staff.

Having given the gift of the body, one should thereafter undertake the practice;

The yogin of great compassion should move about by means of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.

Compassion is constantly drunk for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings.

If one should show a single finger, it means "you have arrived";

One should recognize the Kṣema-mudrā by the pressing of the left thumb. To one to whom the ring finger is offered, one should offer the little finger; to one who shows the middle fingers, one should offer the index finger. (2–3)
To one who shows the ring finger, one should show the neck;
to one who shows the cloth, one should show the trident;
to one who shows the breast, one should show the boundary markers.

Whatever the yoginīs say, all that indeed must be done.
Vajragarbha said:

The Blessed One said:

chandoha and upacchandoha, and likewise melāpaka and upamelāpaka."
Pīlava, upapīlava, śmaśāna, and upaśmaśānaka—(10) these are the twelve stages.

The field renowned as Munmuni, the field of Kāruṇyapāṭaka,

"O Blessed One, what are those days?
The Blessed One said:
"On the fourteenth and likewise on the eighth day of the fortnight of the hungry ghosts. (20)
One should eat a banner, or even that which has been struck by a weapon, and consume [the flesh of] a seven-times-coiled [serpent].

In the subduing of the wicked, everything is accomplished through the primary ritual procedure.

for here, there is nothing inconceivable and nothing that should not be spoken, whether auspicious or inauspicious.

one is formed by the filaments, and the other is heard to be formed by the triangle. (3)
In the center of that, one should contemplate the corpse consisting of fifteen seats;
above that shall be the moon, and above the moon, the seed-syllable.

(5) From the union of the moon and the sun, Gaurī and the others are proclaimed.

The examination of one’s own deity by means of seed-syllables and signs is thus described.
Through all [these], there is a single practice: accomplishment is the nature of purity.
The wise one should cultivate the forms according to the fivefold methods that have been taught.
The union of *āli* and *kāli* is the seat of Vajrasattva.
(8) For the mass arising from the syllables, the utterances *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* are not desired;

All these are renowned as being like the Yoginī Nairātmyā:
their single hand is occupied with a skull-cup, and they hold a ritual knife in the right;
with a khaṭvāṅga in the left, their hips are covered with a tiger skin. (18)
Mounted upon corpses, blazing with radiance, two-armed, and with tawny hair;
likewise, they stand with razors to cut away the six defects, such as pride and the rest.
With the head of one who conceptualizes existence and non-existence, one holds a lotus vessel;
(20) and the blood of the four Māras is drunk for the sake of accomplishment.
It is fashioned through the means of a corpse, by way of the *kaṭvāṅga* and the aspects of emptiness. (21)
By this one should meditate upon the wheel and swiftly attain accomplishment.
One should meditate on the black [form] in the first [moment], and the red indeed in the second;
one should meditate on the yellow in the third, and likewise the green in the fourth.
In the fifth [stage] she is blue-colored, and in the sixth she has a white body.
The yogin should meditate on the six limbs, and likewise again up to the stage of cessation;
indeed, both the sequential generation stage and the completion stage.
The Vajra-holder taught the Dharma by relying upon two stages:
the stage of generation has been explained; now I shall explain the stage of completion.
Regarding the phrase "in the space-element," it refers to the lotuses; "wisdom" is known as the *bhaga*.
Meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is meditative attainment (*samāpatti*); its bliss is called the wheel. Bodhicitta, which is to be personally realized according to the proper method, is the deity;
as it arises, the semen becomes twofold, and from that, the innate (*sahaja*) [bliss] occurs. (26–27)
The woman is indeed wisdom (*prajñā*), while the man is traditionally held to be skillful means (*upāya*).
Subsequently, there is a twofold division of these two based on the distinction between the manifest (*vivṛti*) and the concealed (*saṃvṛti*).
First, regarding the man, there is a twofold division: his semen and his bliss.
And just as in wisdom there is semen in the man and his bliss, so too here is the differentiation of the four joys;
for from the perspective of the *utpannakrama* stage, the innate (*sahaja*) is fourfold. (29–30)
Ānanda is the first hero; Paramānanda is the Yoginī;
Suratananda is the totality [of these]. He who knows all is the means for that bliss. (31) Through Ānanda there is some pleasure; Paramānanda is greater than that.
Through cessation, detachment arises; from the remainder, coemergent bliss [is attained].
(32) The first [joy] is through the longing for touch; the second is through the desire for pleasure;
the third is due to the destruction of passion; by that, the fourth is cultivated. (33)
Existence is said to be supreme bliss, and nirvāṇa is characterized by dispassion;
however, the innate (*sahaja*) is devoid of these, consisting merely of intermediate bliss.
There is neither passion nor dispassion, and the intermediate is not perceived.
Herein there is neither wisdom nor means, because of the perfect awakening to reality.
(35) The innate is not described by another, nor is it found in anything else; it is known by oneself through merit and service to the lineage of gurus. (36)
Those things which are inferior, middling, or superior, and whatever others there may be—
all these should be viewed as equal by those who cultivate reality.
The inferior is said to be a subtle object, while the superior is called a state of being.
Excluding the middle one from the two [extremes], the others are the six sense-faculties.
Whatever is stable or moving, all these are indeed what I have taught.
"Equal" means having identical activities through meditations on reality (*tattvabhāvanā*) that are of a single flavor (*samarasa*).
"Equal" (*sama*) is said to mean "identical" (*tulya*); its "wheel" (*cakra*) is traditionally known as "flavor" (*rasa*).
Thus, by this meaning, "of one flavor" (*samarasa*) is spoken of as being of a single nature (*ekabhāva*). (39–40)
For this entire world originates from me; the three worlds originate from me.
This whole universe is pervaded by me; no world is seen to consist of anything else.
Having realized this, the yogi who is well-composed in practice—
That person succeeds without a doubt, even if they are one of meager merit.
Whether eating, drinking, bathing, awake, or asleep, one who desires the Mahāmudrā should contemplate [this] constantly; through that, they attain it. (42–43)

For the entire world is conceptualized by the mind; that which is not conceptualized is the thorough knowledge of all phenomena—this is cultivation, and not merely cultivation. (44) As for those entities, whether stable or moving, such as grass, shrubs, and creepers...
Indeed, they cultivate the supreme reality, which is the very nature of the self’s being.
For them, there is no other supreme state; it is the great bliss to be personally realized.
Accomplishment is to be personally realized, for cultivation is indeed personal realization.
Action consists of that which is self-cognizable; from affliction, action arises.
One is oneself the destroyer, oneself the doer, oneself the king, and oneself the lord.
Passion, hatred, as well as envy, delusion, and likewise pride—these are the mind.
All of them do not equal even a sixteenth part of that delightful state.

(48) The wisdom arising from the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), which is equal to space and endowed with its means, gives birth to the three worlds therein by virtue of its nature as wisdom and means. (49)
The Blessed One takes the form of semen, and that bliss is known as the beloved woman.
This is the union of the one and the many; from that moment arises the supreme delight.
This gnosis is to be personally realized, its sphere transcending the path of words.

For this is the sequence of empowerment, consisting entirely of the wisdom of the Omniscient One. (51) Earth, water, wind, fire, and space—none of these can, in an instant, obstruct the cognition of one’s own and others’ consciousness. (52)
In an instant, one may become a single form with those in heaven, among mortals, and in the netherworlds;
one cannot be obstructed by the conceptualization of self and other.
(53) [This is] through all the established doctrines of the Vedas, such as the unfolding of ritual actions.
There would be no accomplishment; through purification alone, there would be rebirth in another existence. (54) Without that [knowledge], there is no accomplishment in this world or the next.
For one by whom Hevajra is not known, their exertion is in vain. (55)
Like the flow of a river's current or the continuity of a lamp's flame,
one should remain constantly engaged in the yoga of reality throughout day and night. (56)

the six sense faculties, the five aggregates, the six sense bases, and the five elements.
Though pure by its very nature, it is obscured by ignorance and the afflictions.
(2) Purity is of the nature of self-awareness; one is not liberated through the purification of [external] things.

Why?
Because of the state of the grasped and the grasper.
Vajragarbha asked:

The Blessed One said: Form is perceived by the eye; sound is heard by the ear; one smells fragrance with the nose; and they know that tasting is done by the tongue. (6)
An object is touched by the body, and the mind attains pleasure and so forth;
these should be cultivated as objects of service once they have been rendered poisonless through purification. (7) Vajrā is present in the aggregate of form, and Gaurī is remembered in sensation.
In perception she is Vāriyoginī, and in mental formations she is Vajraḍākinī.
Nairātmyayoginī abides in the form of the aggregate of consciousness.
Indeed, through the constant purification of these [aggregates], the practitioners of reality attain accomplishment.
The inner enclosure. (9) Hereafter, I shall describe the outer enclosure and the yoginīs beginning with Aparagaurī:
Pukkasī is renowned in the northeast, and Śavarī is proclaimed in the southeast.

these two deities abide by way of the nature of both cyclic existence and nirvāṇa. (12)
Gaurī is proclaimed to be in form, and Caurī is celebrated in sound;

For it is through the constant purity of these that the practitioners of reality achieve accomplishment.
(14) The purity of the arms is emptiness; the purity of the feet is from the purification of Māra;

Earth is known as Pukkasī, and the water element is remembered as Śavarī;
fire should be understood as Caṇḍālī, and wind is proclaimed as Ḍombī.
Nairātmyā is designated as Hatred, and Vāriyoginī as Passion.
Envy is Vajraḍākinī, and malice is Guptagaurikā; (17) likewise, Delusion is known as Vajrā. These are the purification of hatred and the other afflictions;
by means of this, the aggregates are purified from the perspective of the generation stage. (18)
By whatever means the world is bound, by those very same means one should release that bondage.
The world is deluded; it does not know reality, and being devoid of reality, it shall not attain accomplishment.
Therefore: (19) There is no smell, no sound, no form, nor indeed taste, nor purity of mind;
no touch, no phenomena—through the purity of all things, I consider the world to be of a pure nature. (20)

Intermingled with wisdom and means, and blended with passion and its absence;

Self, living being, sentient being, time, and even the person—

Bathed, pure, with fragrant limbs, adorned with variegated ornaments,

"The waveless self whose essence is its own true form is established within the entire body. (36)
Vajragarbha said:

The Bhagavat replied: (37)
By means of the union of *bola* and *kakkola*, the practitioner produces *kunduru*;
through the quality of hardness arising from contact, earth is produced therein. (38) And from the liquid form of the *bodhicitta*, the element of water indeed arises.
From friction, fire is produced; from movement, wind is proclaimed.
Pleasure and the space-element are enveloped by these five.
Therefore, that bliss which is called reality is not a great element (*mahābhūta*), because bliss [arises] from it.

its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is declared to be the co-nate, the single vow in all its aspects. (40–41)
The yogin becomes the means of compassion through the separation from causes;
it is known as the *bodhicitta* inseparable from emptiness and compassion.
(42) There is no recitation of mantras, no austerity, and no fire-offering.
There is neither the mandala-member nor the mandala;
that is the recitation of mantra, that is austerity, that is the fire-oblation,
that is the mandala-member, and that is the mandala.
In brief, he is embodied as the assembly of mind.

Attraction occurs in the right part, with two *puttalīs* above;
the gaze for paralyzing is in the middle, and two [fingers] are between the nose and the palate.

Through the practice of six months, one attains perfection; there is no doubt in this matter.
One should not entertain delusion here, for the miraculous powers of the Buddhas are inconceivable.
