One should not perform killing here; it would result only in a breach of the samaya.
(6) Every improper act should be performed, with the sole exception of deceiving a sentient being.
The accomplishment of the mudrā is not attained merely by harming sentient beings. (7)
There, being composed, one should consume the *samaya* substance while it is blazing;
[the syllables] beginning with *na*, *ga*, and *ha*, ending with *śva*, or beginning with *śva*.
Likewise, the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) are to be consumed in the Hevajra [tantra] for the sake of attaining accomplishment.
Then, one should observe seven revolutions by means of the characteristics described in the *Hevajra*.
In the seventh revolution, there occurs the accomplishment that transcends the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*).
Possessing a beautiful voice and clear vision, with a fragrant body and a great form—(10) seven shadows shall appear for him; seeing this, the yogi should recognize it.
By merely consuming it, the state of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*) shall arise in an instant. (11)
Now I shall describe the sādhana of Kurukullā, by which all sentient beings are brought under control.
It was previously taught in brief; here it is set forth in detail according to twelve kalpas.
(12) The goddess arises from the syllable *hrīḥ*, is red in color, and has four arms.
Holding a bow and arrow in her hands and bearing a blue lotus and a hook,
by the mere meditation upon her, one may bring the three worlds under control:
kings by a single hundred thousand recitations, and the common people by ten thousand.
The Paśus, Yakṣas, and so forth [attain success] with ten million [recitations]; the Asuras with seven hundred thousand;
the Devas with two hundred thousand; and the Mantrins with one hundred.
The first King of Rituals, titled *Śrī Hevajra-Ḍākinījālasamvara-Vajragarbha-abhisambodhi*, is completed.
Part II, Chapter i. Then Vajragarbha said:
"May you teach, according to the proper method, the auspicious characteristics of consecration."
The Blessed One, whose essence is the adamantine core, is the singular synthesis of all Buddhas.
(1) The Blessed One said: Having performed the fire offering as prescribed and having completed the mandala,
At dusk, having fashioned the image, one should perform the consecration and other rites.
One who is united with his chosen deity and has mastered the manifest mantras should cause all the Buddhas residing in the sky to enter the heart of the image. (2–3)
Oṃ vajrapuṣpe āḥ hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ vajradhūpe āḥ hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ vajradīpe āḥ hūṃ svāhā |
Oṃ vajragandhe āḥ hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ vajranaivedye āḥ hūṃ svāhā | One should present flowers and other offerings produced from various *hūṃ* syllables.
The offerings of *argha*, *pādya*, and so forth are performed as before, according to the sequence of procedures in the previous tantra.
(5) For pacification (*śāntika*), the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is circular; for enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), it is square;
for killing (*māraṇa*), it is said to be triangular; one should accomplish the remaining rites right here [in these shapes]. (6)
For pacifying rites (*śāntika*), it should be one cubit or half a cubit in height and width;
for enriching rites (*pauṣṭika*), two cubits by one cubit is considered appropriate.
For killing rites (*māraṇa*), it should be twenty finger-breadths by half that measure in height and width.
It should be white in color for pacification, and likewise yellow for enrichment;
black in color for killing, and red is proclaimed for subjugation.
As it is for subduing, so it is for summoning; as it is for hatred and the like, so it is for killing.
(9) For pacification, sesame is used; for nourishment, curd; and likewise, for killing, thorn-apple.
Thorn-apple is prescribed for hatred and the like, while the blue lotus is used for subduing and summoning. (10)
Oṃ! To Agni, of great splendor, who fulfills all desires;
you who act for the benefit of sentient beings out of compassion, be present here!
This is the mantra for the invocation of Agni. (11)
O Goddess, you are the witness, worshipped by the wrathful Hevajra;
O Sustainer who wears various jewels, I, [name], shall draw the mandala.
Go, O Consumer of Oblations, to accomplish both my own welfare and that of others! (12)
"You shall come at the proper time; grant me all accomplishments. This is the mantra for propitiating Agni: (13) oṃ jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hāḥ khaṃ raṃ.
The *argha* mantra:
Oṃ nī rī hūṃ khaḥ. The *pādya* mantra: [Oṃ nī rī hūṃ khaḥ].
Oṃ dhvaṃ dhvaṃ dhvaṃ. This is the mantra for the food offering (*naivedya*).
Chapter One: The Determination of the Fire Offering (*homa*) and the Consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
Part II. Chapter ii. Vajragarbha said:
"Just as a gourd [floats] upon the ocean among all phenomena which are like space,"
"How do sentient beings achieve accomplishment in the form of their chosen deity?
The Blessed One replied:
"By means of the yoga of selflessness, or else through the yoga of Heruka."
One who desires accomplishment should not remain for even a moment with a distracted mind.
(2) A pure place should indeed be prepared for the time of initial practice; staying there, the practitioner of mantra, single-minded and composed, attains success. (3)
In his own home at night, with the thought "I am accomplished," the wise one should meditate upon the Yoginī or else upon the form of Śrī Heruka.
While washing his feet, eating, and chewing betel after rinsing his mouth, he should remain thus.
Rubbing his hands with sandalwood paste, covering his loins with a loincloth, speaking whatever words came to mind while going, standing, being angry, or laughing— (5) 46.
The wise practitioner, observing the vow, should serve the Bhagavatī and meditate upon the Yoginī.
(6) Those who desire accomplishment and strive for success must, with effort, never remain even for a moment in another form or with a mind defiled by ignorance, according to the Buddhas. (7)
"Vajragarbha, for the sake of accomplishment, you should examine for one fortnight— even out of curiosity— the meditation known as 'Illusion' which destroys all defilements,
having abandoned all thought with a mind focused on the form of the deity. (8)
Having cultivated this for one uninterrupted day, you should examine it:
(9) there is no other means in saṃsāra for the accomplishment of the welfare of oneself and others;
knowledge practiced even once produces immediate conviction. (10)
The practitioner is not afflicted at all by fears, madnesses, sufferings, or calamities such as the pain of grief,
nor by passion, hatred, and great delusion. Thus, indeed, one should reflect upon the arising of the fruits of what is beneficial and what is harmful.
How could even a single moment of those yogins exist in Raurava?
[This applies to] those who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution and those who are devoted to the slaughter of living beings;
yet even more so for those of low birth, the foolish, and those who perform cruel deeds. (12–13)

Even those who are ugly and have deformed limbs will achieve success through meditation, provided they practice the ten virtues, are devoted to the guru, have conquered their senses, and are free from pride and anger; such a person will certainly attain success. (14)
Having attained accomplishment through the yoga of constant practice, he remains concentrated.
(15) He should wander in secret for one month until the mudrā is obtained; then the mantra-practitioner receives an instruction and is directed by the yoginīs. (16)
"O Vajradhṛk, having taken such-and-such a mudrā, act for the benefit of sentient beings!
Having obtained that large-eyed woman, adorned with beauty and youth, one should prepare her—blended with *sihlaka* and camphor—with the *bodhicitta*. (17)

Beginning with the ten wholesome actions, one should proclaim the Dharma to her. (18) With a mind focused on the form of the deity and the observance of the pledge with one-pointedness of mind, she will become capable within a single month; of this there is no doubt. (19)
Since a woman who has obtained a boon is free from all conceptual constructions, or else, by means of her own power, she should draw forth and fashion the mudrā.
[She is superior] even to gods, asuras, humans, yakṣas, and kinnaras. (20)
Having grasped that, one should practice the conduct out of confidence in one's own fortitude.
This conduct, which is proclaimed to be of terrifying form, is not said to arise from sensory enjoyment;
rather, it is for the purpose of examining one's own mind: "Is the mind stable or is it unsteady? (21–22)
"Since a yogin must always abide in the form of the deity," Vajragarbha asked:
"For one engaged in the yoga of Nairātmyā, how is the meaning of the mudrā distinguished?"
"If there are two mudrās for each mudrā, how can the accomplishment of the mudrā come about?
The Blessed One said:
Having abandoned the female form, one should assume another form of the Blessed One.
Having discarded the breast, it becomes the *bola*, situated in the midst of the *kakkola*.
The two banks become the bell (*ghaṇṭā*), and the filaments become the *bolaka*.
The remaining form belongs to the Great Being Heruka, the Great Rapture.
(25) For a person engaged in the yoga of Heruka, masculinity is attained effortlessly;
for the yogin whose power is manifest, the accomplishment of the mudrā shall come to pass. (26)
Through both arising and dissolution, wisdom and means are not impaired;
for means is origination, while wisdom is the end of existence.
Therefore, in reality, there is neither dissolution nor arising for it. (27)
Someone is brought to the end of dissolution, yet there is no destruction because of the absence of dissolution.

(28) Through the yoga of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), the practitioner should meditate upon the phenomenal world (*prapañca*); having made the phenomenal world like a dream, he should become free from the phenomenal through the very phenomena themselves. (29)
Just as an illusion, just as a dream, and just as the intermediate state (antarābhava) may appear,
so too does the maṇḍala shine forth through the yoga of constant practice. (30) Just as the great bliss is known during the Mahāmudrā consecrations, [so it shines forth].
That very power belongs to him alone; the maṇḍala does not arise from anything else.
(31) Bliss is black, bliss is yellow, bliss is red, bliss is white;
bliss is dark-brown, bliss is blue, and bliss is the entire world of the moving and the unmoving. (32)
Bliss is wisdom, bliss is the means, and likewise bliss is that which arises from *kunduru*.
Bliss is existence, bliss is non-existence; Vajrasattva is remembered as bliss. (33) Vajragarbha said:
This yoga of the completion stage is considered to be true bliss, the great bliss.
For one who is devoid of the cultivation of the completion stage, what is the purpose of the generation stage?
The Blessed One said: "Aho!"
"Through the force of faith, this Great Bodhisattva has vanished.
In the absence of a body, how can there be happiness? It is impossible to speak of happiness; the world is pervaded by a bliss that exists in the form of both the pervaded and the pervader. (35)

Just as fragrance supported by a flower is not perceived when the flower is absent, so too bliss is not apprehended in the absence of form and the other [sensory objects]. (36) I am not a non-entity, nor am I an entity; I am the Buddha because of the awakening to reality.
Those fools who do not know me, and those who are overcome by laziness—
(37) I dwell in Sukhāvatī, within the bhaga of the true Vajra-woman, in the form of the letter E, the jewel-casket of the Buddhas. (38)
I am the expounder, I am the Dharma; accompanied by the Suganas, I am the listener.
I am that which is to be accomplished, the Teacher of the world; I am the world, and I am also that which belongs to the world. (39)

I am of the nature of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), the ultimate beyond the cessation (*virama*) and so forth; and likewise, O son, the cognition [arises] like a lamp in the darkness. (40) The Teacher possesses the thirty-two marks and the Lord possesses the eighty minor characteristics.
He is established in the female organ within Sukhāvatī under the name Śukra.
(41) Without him there would be no bliss; and apart from bliss, he would not exist. Because of his dependence and lack of independence, bliss arises through union with the deity. (42)
Therefore, the Buddha would not be an existent entity, nor indeed would he be of the nature of non-existence;
for he possesses the forms of arms and faces, yet is formless by virtue of supreme bliss.
Therefore, the entire world is innate, and it is called the innate intrinsic nature.

Nirvāṇa is one's very own nature when the mind has the aspect of purity. However, the form of the deity-yoga is established as soon as [the body] is born; yet, due to the positions of the arms, faces, and colors, there remains the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the ordinary state. (44–45)
By the very same piece of poison by which all living beings die,
one who knows the true nature of poison may expel that poison with poison itself.
Or, just as food made of black gram is given to one seized by wind.
Wind is cured by wind through the application of contrary medicines;
existence is purified by existence itself through the counteracting of conceptual constructions.
Just as water that has entered the ear is drawn out by means of more water.
In the same way, conceptualization regarding existence is indeed purified by means of its various forms.
Just as things burnt by fire are steamed again by fire, so too those burnt by the fire of passion are steamed by the fire of passion. (48–49)
For by whatever fierce karma sentient beings are bound, by that very same means they are released from the bondage of existence. (50) The world is bound by passion; by passion alone it is liberated.
Indeed, this inverted cultivation has not been understood by the Buddhist heretics.
(51) In the *kundura* [the sexual organ], there are five according to the nature of the five elements;
yet that which is the single Great Bliss becomes fivefold through its divisions. (52)
Through the union of the *bola* and *kakkola*, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of solidity arises from touch;
since that which is solid has the nature of delusion (*moha*), delusion is considered to be Vairocana.
(53) Since the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) is fluid, it is considered to be the water element (*abdhātu*).
Because water is of an unshakeable nature, Hatred is indeed Akṣobhya-nāyaka. (54) From the friction and conjunction of two [substances], fire is always produced;
Passion shall be Amitavajra, for Passion arises from fire. (55)
The mind that resides in the *kakkolaka* is of the nature of wind (*samīraṇa*).
Envy is indeed Amoghasiddhi; for Amogha arises from wind. Pleasure is passion (*rāga*), and the one who is impassioned (*rakta*) has attachment (*rakti*), which is characterized by space (*ākāśa*).
Space is the Vajra of Slander; slander arises from space.
The single, great mind exists in five forms.
Therein, within the five families, there are births numbering many thousands.
Therefore, that single-natured supreme and eternal great bliss becomes fivefold through the differentiation of the five mental states, such as passion and the rest. (58–59)
In each single family, there are as many assemblies of Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in ten Ganges rivers; indeed,
within those families of assemblies, there are many further families.
Within those families there are hundreds of families;
and those hundreds of thousands of families become many millions of families.

In those families, there are countless families born from the family of supreme bliss. (61) In the *Hevajra*, the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*, this is the second chapter, titled "The Determination of Siddhis."
Part II, Chapter III.
Then the Vajrī spoke this means for the yoginīs, titled "The Source of All Tantras," concerning the *saṃvara*, the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), and likewise the intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣa*).
And likewise, the distinctions of the moments of bliss (*ānandakṣaṇabheda*) and other things such as food;
regarding that, he speaks of the vow (*saṃvara*):
"The vow of all the Buddhas is established in the *evaṃkāra*."
Through consecration, one correctly knows that the syllable *evaṃ* is great bliss.
Then the yoginīs said this to the Blessed One, Vajrasattva:
"What is called the syllable *evaṃ*, and what is the *saṃvara* of the ḍākinīs?"
May the Blessed One, the Teacher, the Guru of the World, teach according to the proper method.
The Blessed One said:
"That which is divine, shaped like the letter E, adorned in its center with the syllable Vaṃ."
The *ālaya* is the repository of all blisses, a jewel-casket of the Buddhas. (4) Therein, joys arise, differentiated according to the distinctions of moments.
Through the knowledge of the moment, the knowledge of bliss is established in the syllable Evaṃ. (5)
The diverse (*vicitra*), the ripening (*vipāka*), the crushing (*vimarda*), and likewise the distinctive (*vilakṣaṇa*):
thus do yogins know that which is to be attained through these four moments. (6) "Diverse" is known as manifold, consisting of embracing, kissing, and so forth.
The maturation is its opposite; it is the enjoyment of the knowledge of bliss.
Contemplation is said to be the "churning," [the thought] "bliss has been enjoyed by me."
The "distinctive" (*vilakṣaṇa*) is other than the three [preceding states], free from both passion and the absence of passion.
(8) The "extraordinary joy" (*vicitrānanda*) is the giver of the first [joy]; the "supreme joy" (*paramānanda*) is in the ripening (*vipākaka*);
the "joy of cessation" (*viramānanda*) is in the dissolution (*vimarda*); and the "innate joy" (*sahajānanda*) is in the distinctive state. (9)
The Master, the Secret, and Wisdom, and likewise the Fourth;
these joys are to be known in sequence by the number of the four sprinklings. Through the purification of laughter, one is the Master; through gazing, likewise the Secret One.
For wisdom (*prajñā*) is for the attainment of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and that [attainment] occurs again through the system of the couple (*dvandva*).
(11) The fourfold consecration (*seka*) is proclaimed for the sake of the accomplishment of sentient beings.
It is called "consecration" (*sekas*) because by means of it one is sprinkled (*sicyate*) or bathed (*snāpyate*). (12)
Embracing with both hands a Prajñā of sixteen years, through the union of the bell and the vajra, the consecration by the Ācārya is considered [to be performed].
She has a beautiful face, large eyes, and is adorned with beauty and youth. (13)
One should cause [the substance] to fall from the thumb and ring finger into the mouth of the disciple.
There, within the very sphere of the disciple, the equal flavor (samarasa) must be brought about.
The Teacher should worship the Prajñā, and having honored her, he should offer her [to the disciple]. (14–15)

The Teacher should say: "O Mahāsattva, take up the mudrā that brings happiness, having recognized the disciple as one who has become great, free from envy, and devoid of anger. (16) The Teacher commands him: "O Vajradhṛk, perform the *kundura*!"
I shall now declare the duties of the disciple and how one should lead him toward consecration.
Upon seeing the Guru endowed with the mudrās, one should perform praise and worship as follows:
"O Blessed One, Great Peaceful One, solely intent upon the Vajrayoga! (17–18)
O Lord, you who have arisen from the indivisible vajra-yoga that perfects the mudrās—just as you are great-souled, so too act for me!
I am submerged in the mire of saṃsāra; protect me, who am without refuge. (19)
With sweet foods, drinks, and edibles, as well as intoxicants and great strength;
with incense, food offerings, garlands, bells, banners, and ointments—with these acts of worship and the like, the disciple should worship the Holder of the Vajra. (20–21)
When the moment of supreme bliss, devoid of manifoldness, has been attained, the Teacher should say: "O Great Being, you must maintain this great bliss.
O Vajradhara, act for the sake of sentient beings until the end of enlightenment. (22)
Thus spoke the Vajra-holder, gazing upon his disciple with a mass of compassion:
(23) "This very Great Wisdom is established within all bodies;
it is the Lord who is non-dual yet possesses a dual form, and whose nature consists of both existence and non-existence. (24)
Pervading all that is stable and moving, it remains present and shines forth in the form of *māyā*;
through the means of the maṇḍala, the wheel, and so forth, it attains constant certainty. (25)
Then Vajragarbha, having consoled all the yoginīs and sisters, spoke thus to the Blessed One:
"What is called the maṇḍala-circle, the city consisting of the essence of all Buddhas? May the Blessed Ones teach it according to the proper method; for a delusion has arisen in me. (26)

The Blessed One said: "Maṇḍala" is said to be the essence, the great bliss of the awakened mind (*bodhicitta*). Because it takes that [essence] up, it is considered a *maṇḍala*; it is thought of as "grinding" (*malana*). (27)
The wheel is the assembly known as the space-element, which is the purification of the sense objects and so forth.
Through the union of *bola* and *kakkola*, his bliss is perceived.
Vajragarbha asked: "By what commitment (*samaya*) should one abide, and by what vow (*saṃvara*)?"
The Blessed One said:
"Living beings must be killed by you, and false speech must be spoken;
what is not given must be taken by you, and you must consort with the wives of others. (29)
The taking of life is said to be a single state of mind, since the vital breath is considered to be the mind; I shall deliver the worlds from what is called false speech;
the emission of the woman's seed is theft, and the wives of others are one's own consort, the beautiful Svābhā. (30)
Then all the yoginīs spoke thus to the Blessed One:
What, then, are those objects, what are the sense faculties, what is the sphere, and how are the aggregates?
What, then, are those elements? What is their intrinsic nature?
The Blessed One said:
The six objects:
form, sound, likewise smell, taste, and touch, as well as that which has the nature of the dharma-element—these six are considered the objects. (32)
And there are six sense faculties:
the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and likewise the mind;
these six sense faculties are joined with Mohavajrā and the others. (33)
And through the distinctions of objects and subjects, there are the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
O Great Compassionate One, there are also the five aggregates (*skandha*) beginning with form and ending with consciousness.
Furthermore, there are the sense faculties, their objects, and the consciousnesses of those faculties.
The eighteen elements have been taught for the awakening of the yoginīs.
Their intrinsic nature is primordially unarisen; likewise, it is neither true nor false.
All things are like the moon reflected in water—thus do the yoginīs know them according to their will. (35–36)

For example, fire arises suddenly in dependence upon the fire-drill, the wood to be drilled, and the exertion of a person’s hands. That fire does not abide in the fire-drill, nor in the wood to be drilled, nor in the exertion of a person’s hands; for when thoroughly sought in every way, it is not found even in a single one of them. And that fire is neither real nor unreal. In this same way, O Yoginīs, attend to all phenomena. (37)

Then all the Vajra-Ḍākinīs, headed by the Yoginī Nairātmyā, taking the five nectars and the sacramental substance (*samayadravya*), worship the Blessed One Vajrasattva. Through the yoga of *kunduru*, they cause him to experience passion and make him drink the essence of the vajra-amrita.
Thereafter, when the Blessed One is satisfied, they display their empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
O Vajraḍākinīs!
This reality, which has been kept secret by me and is honored by all the Buddhas, I shall proclaim through the power of the vajra-worship; listen with desire. (39)
Then all the goddesses, filled with enthusiasm, placed their right knees upon the ground, bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One, and listened to what the Blessed One had said.
The Blessed One said:
"One should not avoid food or drink as they are obtained, nor should one distinguish between what is permissible and what is forbidden."

One should not perform ritual bathing or purification, nor should one avoid sexual intercourse with a village woman. (41) The wise person should not recite mantras, nor should he rely upon meditative concentration.
He should not abandon sleep, nor should he restrain his senses. (42)
One should practice the consumption of all powers of the five colors;
one sports with every woman with a mind free from hesitation. (43) One should not cultivate affection for friends, nor likewise hatred toward enemies.
One should not pay homage to these deities made of wood, stone, or clay;
for a yogin must always abide as the embodiment of the deity itself.
[One should likewise avoid] those who are untouchable, such as Dombas, Caṇḍālas, leather-workers, and Haḍḍikas.
One should touch Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others as if they were one's own body.
[One should likewise touch] the five nectars, molasses, wine, poison, neem, that which is born of childbirth, the sour, sweet, and astringent, as well as the bitter, salty, and pungent. (45–46)
One should consume putrid things, fragrances, water, and blood with the *bodhicitta*;
there is nothing that cannot be consumed by one whose mind possesses non-dual gnosis.
Having obtained the self-arisen flower, one should place it within the vessel of the lotus.
The observer of the vow, having mixed phlegm and nasal mucus together, should drink them.
(48) Having obtained a multi-colored loincloth and ornaments made of clay and salt from a cemetery, he should bind excellent hair with flowers found there. (49)
Then Vajragarbha said:
"The sense faculties are indeed unrefined and established as being six in number;
yet the Blessed One previously taught the purification of all their objects. (50)
The Blessed One said:
"Delusion-vajra is in the eyes, and Hatred-vajri is in the two ears."
Mātsaryakī is renowned for the nose, and Rāgavajrikā for the mouth;
(51) Īrṣyāvajrā is for touch, and Nairātmyayoginī is for the mind.
O Mahāsattva, this armor [is formed] by these [deities] for the purification of the sense faculties. (52)
Vajragarbha said:

"O Blessed One, please explain with certainty what is called 'twilight language' (*sandhyābhāṣa*), the great commitment (*mahāsamaya*) of the yoginīs, which is not breached by the Śrāvakas and others. (53)
Smiling with the eyes, as well as embracing in pairs, and even by means of the fourfold tantra— this is the sandhyābhāṣā, which is not expressed in literal words. (54) The Blessed One said:

I shall speak, O Vajragarbha; listen with a one-pointed mind to the intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣa*), the great language (*māhābhāṣa*), and the detailed exposition of the conventions of the pledge (*samaya*). Intoxication is wine, strength is meat, and union is considered to be sandalwood.
Gati is kheṭa, śava is śrāya, and bone-ornament is niraṃśuka. (56) Āgati is said to be preṅkhaṇa, and kṛpīṭa is considered to be ḍamaruka.
Abhavya is known as dundura, and bhavya is considered to be kāliñjara. (57)
The drum is said to be the untouchable; the skull is the lotus-vessel.
The food is to be known as that which provides satisfaction; the side-dish is the fuel of *mālatī*. (58) Excrement is said to be the four-fold equalizer (*catuḥsama*); urine is remembered as musk.
Svayaṃbhu is to be known as sihlaka, and śukra is considered to be karpūraka.
Mahāmāṃsa is declared to be sālija, and the union of the two organs is kunduru.
Vajra is renowned as bolaka, and padma is considered to be kakkolaka. (59–60)
The family is known to be fivefold, divided according to the distinction of castes;
thus, through the twilight language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*), the Buddhas are the five *kaulikās*.
The *ḍombī* is known as belonging to the Vajra family, and likewise the *naṭī* belongs to the Padma family.

The Caṇḍālī is considered to belong to the Jewel family, and the Brāhmaṇī to the Tathāgata family; (62) the Rajakī belongs to the Action family—these mudrās bestow excellent accomplishment. Their seminal essence is the vajra; having worshipped it, the practitioner should drink it. (63)

O Vajragarbha Mahāsattva, whatever I have spoken to you, all of that—wonderful and consisting of intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣa*)—should be received with reverence. He who has been consecrated here in this Hevajra [tantra] and does not speak in intentional language [is at fault]. (64)
The violation of his samaya occurs; of this there is no doubt.
(65) Thus, by calamities, thieves, planets, fevers, poisons, and so forth— 62.
Even he would die if he were a Buddha, should he not speak in the sandhyābhāṣā.
If, having encountered those who know their own samaya, he does not speak these words, then the yoginīs born of the four seats will cause him agitation. (66–67)
The third chapter, titled "The Esoteric Language of the Treasury of All Hevajra Tantras."
Part II, Chapter IV.
Then all the ḍākinīs, headed by Vajragarbha, being filled with doubt and dejected in mind, spoke thus to the Blessed One Vajrasattva:
"May the Blessed One dispel our doubt. (1)
Regarding that which was taught in the Caryāpaṭala—the song and the dance that grant accomplishment—I have a doubt concerning them: what is the song, and what is the dance?
(2) And as for that which was spoken regarding the sealing of Hatred and the other [passions] through the consecration of the deities—
In this regard, a doubt arises within me: what is the seal, and of what is there the sealing?

(3) Regarding that which was taught in the Mantra Chapter concerning the seed-syllable of Nairātmyā and the others, a confusion has arisen in me: what is the seed, and of what is it the seed-syllable? (4)
"Regarding the channels (*nāḍī*) consisting of thirty-two [petals] that are proclaimed in the *Kulapaṭala*, may the Blessed Ones explain their purification; a delusion has arisen in me.
The Blessed One said:
In Kollaïra they speak Bolā, in Mummuṇira Kakkolā;
in Ghaṇakibiḍa they play the Vājja, and in Karuṇe they do not perform Rolā.
(6) There one eats Baru, and in Gāḍa one drinks Maanā.
Fresh *kāliñjara* nuts are traded there, and the *dunduru* drum is sounded;
*caūsama*, *kacchuri*, *sihlā*, and camphor are applied [as perfumes];
*mālaindhana* and *śāliñja* are eaten as food there. (7)
While swinging and playing at ball, they do not distinguish between pure and impure;
having climbed upon the dry limbs, there the wine is sold.
On the path to Malaya and Kundura, the drum is not struck that day. (8)
The dance is performed in the form of Śrī Heruka through the yoga of unclouded mindfulness;
the meditation is performed with a passionate mind and a consciousness of uninterrupted practice.
Thus, by the Vajradharmas, the Buddhas, the Yoginīs, and the Mothers. (9)
By means of these two—song and dance—the Supreme is sung and danced.

(10) By this very [means], the protection of the Gaṇas and likewise the protection of oneself [is achieved]; by this very [means], one gains mastery over the world, and the recitation of mantras is performed by this very [means]. (11)
Where it is sung with devotion and where it is danced with devotion,
placing the Lord of the Gaṇas at the forefront, there one should perceive the sense of smell. (12)
First, one should perceive the scent of garlic, then the vulture-like odor; thereafter, the scent of camphor and that of the *mālayaja* flower, which is the locus of song.
Following the conclusion of the song, the cry of a swan and a bee is heard.
One should also observe the sound of a jackal in the outer garden.
Sealing and the mark of the *liṅga* indicate the family (*kula*) by means of its sign;
if the family is disordered through the yoga of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there is neither accomplishment nor a practitioner.
One should seal Nairātmyā with the seal of hatred, Vajrā with the seal of delusion, Gaurī with the seal of malice, and Vārī with the seal of passion.
One should seal Ḍākinī with the seal of envy and Pukkasī with the seal of hatred. (16)

One should worship Śavarī with the mudrā of delusion, Caṇḍālī with the mudrā of malice, Ḍombī with the mudrā of passion, and again Gaurī with hatred; likewise, Caurī with the mudrā of delusion and Vetālī with the mudrā of malice. (17–18)
One should know the sealing by desire: Ghasmarī with the seal of passion (*rāga*), Bhūcarī with the seal of delusion (*moha*), and Khecarī with the seal of passion.
(19) Nairātmyā is at the beginning of *Aler*, and Vajrāler is the second.

Āle is Tṛtīyakā, Gaurī is the fourth, and Vāriyoginī is the fifth; (20) Vajraḍākī is the sixth, and Pukkasī is considered the seventh; Śavarī is the eighth, and Caṇḍālī is remembered as the ninth. (21)
The ninth is Ḍombinī, and Gaurī again is the tenth;
Caurī is known as the eleventh, and Vetālī is considered the twelfth.
Ghasmarī is the thirteenth, and Bhūcarī is the fourteenth.
The fifteenth is Khecarī, the seed-syllable of the Yoginīs.
(23) Regarding the channels described in the *Kulapaṭala* as being sixteen in number, it is held that each pair of channels corresponds sequentially to one Yoginī. (24)
Lalanā, rasanā, and avadhūtī are considered to be the yoginīs of Nairātmyā.
One should diligently abandon all the remaining [kalās], because the sixteenth kalā does not exist. For what reason? Because it performs purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
Bodhicitta becomes the moon consisting of fifteen digits;
its form is the syllable Āli, which is great bliss, and the yoginīs are its constituent parts.
Vajragarbha said:
Why indeed should camphor— which arises from all yoginīs, whose nature is innate bliss, which is imperishable, abundant, and sky-going— not be abandoned? (27)
The Blessed One said:
It is just as you say.
Vajragarbha said:
By what means should the thought of awakening be generated?
The Blessed One said:
By means of the maṇḍala circle and so forth, and through the process of self-consecration,
one should generate the bodhicitta, which consists of both the absolute and the relative aspects.
The relative [bodhicitta] resembles a jasmine flower, while the absolute has the nature of bliss.
In the *Strīkakkola-saukhāvatī*, which has the nature of the syllable *Evaṃ*, it is called *Sukhāvatī* precisely because it protects bliss;
it is the support for the Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas, and the holders of the Vajra. (30–31)
In this very way is saṃsāra, and in this very way is nirvāṇa. It is said that there is no nirvāṇa other than saṃsāra.
Form, sound, and so forth are saṃsāra; feeling and so forth are saṃsāra.

Cyclic existence is nothing but the sense faculties; cyclic existence consists of hatred and the rest. (33) These very phenomena are nirvāṇa, yet through delusion they take the form of cyclic existence.
One who is undeluded, while still cycling, experiences cyclic existence as nirvāṇa through purity. (34)
Nirvṛti is the bodhicitta, whose nature consists of the absolute and the conventional;
she has a beautiful face and wide eyes, adorned with beauty and youth. (35) She is dark-complexioned, steadfast, of noble lineage, and produced from storax and camphor.

One should cause the consort, who has been consecrated by oneself in Hevajra, who possesses beautiful hair, and who is dear to the practitioner, to drink the intoxicant; then one should drink it oneself. Afterwards, for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of both self and others, one should arouse passion for the mudrā. (36–37)
Having inserted the *bolaka* into the *kakkola*, the observer of the vow produces the *kunduru*.
The wise one should not discard the camphor produced in that yoga;
it should not be grasped with the hand, nor with oyster shells, nor with conch shells. (38)
Amṛta is to be grasped with the tongue for the sake of increasing strength.
Karpūra is indeed Nairātmyā; bliss is the form of Nairātmyā, and her bliss, Mahāmudrā, is situated in the circle of the navel. (39–40)
That wisdom is conceived by the Buddhas as having the nature of the primordial vowel;
she herself is the Blessed Lady Prajñā through the yoga of the *utpannakrama*.
She is neither long nor short, neither square nor circular.
Endowed with the fragrance and taste of its own essence, it produces innate bliss;
therein the yogin arises and enjoys its happiness. (42)
Together with her, there shall be accomplishment, bestowing the bliss of Mahāmudrā.
Form, sound, likewise smell, taste, and touch, as well as the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, are enjoyed through wisdom alone. (43–44)
She alone is the divine Yoginī of great bliss, whose nature is the innate (*sahaja*);
she alone is the mandala-circle, the very embodiment of the five wisdoms.
She is the form of the mirror-like wisdom and she is the realization of the wisdom of equality.
It is indeed the correct analytical investigation and the performance of duties;
it is the perfectly pure realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). It is that very same I, the Lord of the Mandala;
it is that very Nairātmyā Yoginī, whose essential nature is the realm of phenomena.
Vajragarbha said:
"The Blessed One has previously taught the arising of the deities according to the path of meditating on the wheel; now please tell me the *samvara*. (48)
The Blessed One said:
"Situated within the body of the Yoginī, it abides as the vow (*saṃvara*) of the letter A.
Just as it is externally, so too internally is that vow revealed. (49)
The bliss of the *bala* is Mahāmudrā, the Vajra-āyatana which is the means (*upāyaka*).
By means of this secret union (*guhyasamāpatti*), the external duality is demonstrated.
(50) The three bodies (*trikāya*) within the center of the body are said to exist in the form of wheels (*cakra*).

The five wisdoms of the three bodies are considered to be the wheel of great bliss. Likewise, the Dharma, Sambhoga, and Nirmāṇa bodies, as well as great bliss, are established in the yoni, heart, throat, and head respectively. (51–52)
Wherever the birth of all sentient beings without exception is proclaimed, there the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) exists; emanation is considered to be that which is stable.
(53) It is regarded as "emanational" (*nirmāṇika*) because by means of it, one is born or emanated.
Dharma is the very nature of the mind; the Dharmakāya resides in the heart.
Enjoyment is said to be the tasting of the six flavors; the Saṃbhogacakra is at the throat, and Great Bliss is situated at the head. (54–55)

In the *evaṃkāra*, there is the outflow (*niṣyanda*); from the Wheel of Dharma, the ripening (*vipāka*); the human effort (*puruṣakāra*) in the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhoga*); and the stainlessness (*vaimalya*) in the Wheel of Bliss (*sukhacakra*). (56) Thus, the fruit is said to be fourfold, distinguished by the outflow and the others.

The Blessed Lady Prajñā is the enjoyer of karma, impelled by the wind of karma. As it was performed, so it is experienced; this is termed "outflow" (*niṣyanda*). Its opposite is "ripening" (*vipāka*): a great fruit from a small karma.
Human effort, acquisition, and stainlessness through the purity of yoga;
(58) Sthāvarī is in the Nirmāṇacakra because emanation is stable therein.
In the *Sarvāstivāda* [wheel], the discourse on the Dharma arises within the *dharmacakra*;

(59) because consciousness (*saṃvit*) and sensation (*saṃvedana*) reside in the throat as the *saṃbhogacakra*; and because great bliss (*mahāsukha*) resides in the heart as the *mahāsukhacakra*, it is the *Mahāsaṅghī*. (60)
The "nikāya" is said to be the body; it is called a sublime dwelling.
From one free from passion, there arises the womb, the placenta, and the blazing robe.
Likewise, the preceptor and the mother receive salutation with the palms joined at the head.
The training rules, the duties of the world, and likewise the recitation of mantras—these are the day.
(62) The letter *A* is the womb-circle, and the letter *Ha* is great bliss;
born as a monk, he is the mantra of sound, naked, with his head and beard shaven. (63)
By these causal conditions, sentient beings are indeed Buddhas; of this there is no doubt.
The ten stages (*bhūmi*) are the ten months, and sentient beings are the lords of the ten stages.

(64) Then all the goddesses, headed by the Yoginī Nairātmyā—namely, Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, Tārā, Bhṛkuṭī, Cundā, Parṇaśavarī, and Ahomukhā—and other Yoginīs equal in number to the atoms of Mount Sumeru, were struck with supreme wonder. (65)

Having heard these words of Bhāratī, all the goddesses fainted, were terrified, and fell to the ground. Seeing them overcome by fear, the wielder of the thunderbolt (Vajrin) praised them in order to restore them:
"O Earth, Water, Wind, Fire, and Sky, you sister goddesses, listen! I shall speak so that no one may remain ignorant of it. (66–67)
Having heard the Blessed One’s words, which were like a dream, they all regained their lives.
The Blessed One said:
Sentient beings are indeed Buddhas, but they are obscured by adventitious defilements;
by removing those [defilements], sentient beings are undoubtedly Buddhas. (69) The goddesses said:
"So it is, Blessed One; this is true, not false."
The Blessed One said:
(70) "He who eats poison as food and yet does not die, and whose mind is free from delusion and pride—that person truly rejoices in the supreme reality. (71)
Likewise, those who know the means of cessation and have exerted themselves in the *Hevajra* [tantras] are not seized by ignorance and the like, nor by the fetters of delusion and so forth.
(72) There is not a single sentient being who is not awakened, because each and every one has attained self-awakening.
Hell-beings, pretas, animals, gods, asuras, and humans—
even worms in filth and the like— are by their very nature constantly happy.
For they do not know that happiness belongs to both gods and asuras. (74) A Buddha is not found anywhere else in other world-systems;
for the Fully Awakened One is the mind itself—the Buddha is not shown to exist elsewhere. (75)
Even those such as Caṇḍālas and Caṇḍakāras, whose minds are intent on the purpose of killing, attain accomplishment by resorting to Hevajra; there is no doubt in this matter.
Fools, shrouded in ignorance and lacking knowledge, do not understand this path.
Those deluded ones wander through the prison of existence within the six realms of rebirth.
But having obtained the means, O Vajragarbha of great compassion, they purify the sense objects and shall indeed attain the unsurpassed state. (77–78)
Vajragarbha said: "The earth is known as Pukkasī; how then is there the sealing by Akṣobhya?
Since hardness is delusion (moha), the body is considered to be Vairocana."
"Pukkasī is the seal that stamps delusion; O Lord, this sealing is appropriate.
The Blessed One said:
"Apart from the body, the mind has no other play."
Therefore, Vairocana is the mind; one should seal the body with the mind.
Vajragarbha said:
The water element is known as Śabarī, and Akṣobhya has the nature of fluidity.
"O Lord, it is appropriate for the Śavarī to be sealed with the Akṣobhya-mudrā.
The Blessed One said:
"Apart from the mind, no other existence of the body is perceived."
Therefore, the mind should become delusion; one should seal the mind with delusion.
Vajragarbha said:
"Tejas is known as Caṇḍālinī; how is there sealing by means of Ratna?"
It is appropriate for the Caṇḍālī to be sealed by the seal of passion; there is no sealing by any other seal.
The Blessed One said:
"Since passion is known as that which is impassioned, and the impassioned one is Ratnasaṃbhava..."
Because fire has the nature of redness, one should seal passion with malice. (84) Vajragarbha said:
"Because Ḍombinī is the wind, and the wind has the form of Amogha; O Lord, the sealing with the Amogha-mudrā is appropriate for Ḍombinī. (85) The Blessed One said:
Having abandoned passion, there can be no arising of envy elsewhere;
therefore, the wise one should seal the Ḍombinī with the seal of passion.
Since form is solidity, Vairocana is considered the consort of Gaurī.
By the very same principle previously stated, one should seal Gaurī with Citteśa;
likewise, by that same principle, one should seal Caurī, Vetālī, and Ghasmarī according to that method, sealing them without error. (87–88)
While the deity Hevajra, the holder of the vajra, remained in meditative absorption,
Nairātmyā there asked about the great *bali* offering for the sake of sentient beings. Seated within the syllable *Evaṃ*, Vajrasattva shall bestow the *bali*.
For the protection of the lives of sentient beings from obstacles and even from obstructing spirits— [from] Indra, Yama, Jala, Yakṣas,
Bhūtas, Vahni, and Vāyu— may there be protection. (90)
Candra, Sūrya, Māta, Bappa, Talapātāla, Aṣṭasarpa, Svāhā!
(91) Consume this offering; smell it!
With flowers, incense, meat, and blood, accomplish all tasks; practice patience and destroy the firm [obstacles]. (92)
Oṃ, the mouth [of all] has been made, because all phenomena are unarisen from the beginning.
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.

(93) If, by means of this *bali* offering, yogins perform worship to all spirits for the sake of auspiciousness, then there will be untroubled happiness among them; the gods will be satisfied, and there will be well-being for the world. (94)

Subjugation, the destruction of enemies' armies through malevolent rites, expulsion, killing, and summoning—these, as well as pacification, happiness, and nourishment, shall come to pass. If one offers an oblation here to the host of spirits, it will be eternal.
Vajragarbha asked: "By which mudrā is Khecarī [attained], and by whose mudrā is Bhūcarī?"
"O Lord, how was it that I did not previously know that this sealing should be performed?
The Blessed One said:
The triple secret is within the center of the wheel, distinguished by body, speech, and mind;
the lower, upper, and middle positions are established within the center of the wheel.
Bhūcarī is the body-mudrā, facing downward, she who possesses the vajra of the body.
Khecarī, Rāgamudrī, Ūrdhvamukhī, and Vāgvajriṇī;
Cittavajrī and Nairātmyā—mind is the form of selflessness.
Mind is the middle state; therefore, Nairātmyā is born from the middle. (98–99)
They say there are six kinds of families; one should explain them in detail.
They are also said to be threefold and fivefold; listen, O Yoginī!
[The Buddhas are] Akṣobhya, Vairocana, Ratnasambhava, Amitaprabha, Amoghasiddhi, and Vajrasattva. [The afflictions are] hatred, delusion, malice, passion, envy, and bliss. (100–101)
For they are to be cultivated through purification and according to the sequence of the methods.
Setting aside that which is called Vajrasattva, there subsequently follows the fivefold family;
that [fivefold] follows the threefold [division] by means of delusion, passion, and hatred.
But the single family is the Lord of Mind, Akṣobhya, who has the form of hatred. (102)
This is the power of the Vajra of Hatred; the family is considered to be sixfold and fivefold.
(103) This is the fourth chapter, titled "The Summary Meaning of the Sealing of All Tantras of Hevajra."
Part II, Chapter V.
Now, the Lord Hevajra, the Vajra-holder, the Great King, the Bestower of All, whose very nature is the essence of all forms, shall fully reveal the mandala. (1)
Seated in Sukhāvatī, possessing the nature of all forms,
the Lord of the Maṇḍala is perfected from the seed-syllable of Cittavajra.
He has sixteen arms, eight faces, and four feet, and is terrifying.
The goddess Nairātmyā herself asks the Lord, the hero who wears a garland of skulls, whose neck is embraced by Nairātmyā, and who bears the five mudrās: "This wheel of ours,
which you have described as surrounded by fifteen [deities]— "
"O Lord, what is your maṇḍala like? It was not known by me before.
(4) Having kissed Nairātmyā, having placed the vajra within the skull-cup, and having massaged her breasts, the Lord shall reveal the maṇḍala. (5)
The maṇḍala is as previously described, adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces;
it has four corners, four gates, and is embellished with vajra-lines. (6)
There, in the center, I am present together with you, O fair-faced one,
through the passion of great passion, by virtue of the nature of innate bliss.
(7) [I am] eight-faced, four-legged, and adorned with sixteen arms.
Trampled by the four Māras, he is terrifying even to fear itself;
wearing a necklace made of a garland of severed heads, he stands upon the sun in a state of *tāṇḍava* dance;
holding a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) upon his head, he is black in color and fearsome. (8–9)
One should emanate the syllable *HŪṂ* from the mouth [of the deity], whose body is smeared with ashes, who has attained the bliss of sexual union, and who is joined with Nairātmyā;
he has obtained waveless bliss and possesses a waveless nature. (10)
The primary face is deep black, the right is like a jasmine flower, and the left is red and most terrifying;
the face on the crown of the head is formidable, possessing twenty-four eyes and the rest, while the remaining faces resemble bees. (11–12)
While you and I were sporting with intense passion in the beautiful city of old,
Gaurī was emitted and well-established at the eastern gate in the direction of Indra. Furthermore,
by means of the union of the churner and the act of churning, Caurikā was again emitted.
Relying upon the southern gate, that Caurī is the guardian of the door.
(14) Through the union of the *bola* and *kakkola*, Vetālī emerges;
furthermore, Ghasmarī, having emerged at the western gate, sits there as the Destroyer of Māra. (15)
During the great union, Ghasmarī emerged once more;
having emerged, she sat at the northern gate, possessing a fierce form. From the friction and conjunction of the two, Śavarī appeared in the southeast corner.
Caṇḍālī is in the direction of the rākṣasas, and Ḍombī is in the wind-corner (northwest).
(18) Then, from the great passion of the Vajrī, [the seed] becomes liquefied along with the consort;
thereafter, the goddesses urge him on with various songs and offerings. (19)
Arise, O Bharāḍa! O Pukkasī, essence of compassion, protect me!
Abandoning desire through the great union of wisdom (*prajñā*), they remain in empty meditative absorption (*śūnyasamādhi*).
Even though I am thus distressed, I shall die; arise, O Hevajra! (20)
Abandon this void nature, O Śabarī; accomplish your purpose!
(21) Having invited the world, O Lord of the Gods, why do you remain in solitude?
"O Caṇḍālī, I have informed you; I have informed you, yet you are not seen. (22) "O Indīālī, arise! I know your heart."
O Ambhā, O Ḍombī, O Cheamaṇḍa, do not cause the interruption of compassion!

(23) Likewise, the elephant, horse, donkey, cow, camel, human, and sarabha-utuka are to be known by their feet [as the deities] on the eight skull-bowls of the south, starting from the elephants. (24)
Earth, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Fire, the Moon, and the Sun,
as well as Antaka and Dhanada, are the guardians of the eight directions of the left.
[These are associated with] the sentiments of the erotic, the heroic, the loathsome, the furious, the comic, and the terrifying.
Endowed with the sentiments of compassion, wonder, and tranquility, as well as the sentiments of laughter and the rest,
the Great Vajra-holder arises from the liquid form by means of the two syllables *aṃ* and *hūṃ*,
spreading his feet upon the ground and threatening the gods and asuras. (26–27)
One should emanate these [Mothers] by means of the seed-syllables GAṂ, CAṂ, VAṂ, GHAṂ, PAṂ, ŚAṂ, LAṂ, and ḌAṂ;
and [emanate] their lords by means of the seed-syllables HŪṂ and AṂ, which are blue and terrifying with flames.
One should meditate upon such a Lord within the delightful city of the circle of Mothers.
Black in color and most terrible, she bestows happiness upon Nairātmya.
(29) In the right hand of Gaurī is a knife, and likewise in her left is a Rohita fish;
in the right hand of Cauryā is a hoe, and in her left a boar. (30)
To the right of Vetālī is a tortoise, and to her left a lotus vessel;
to the right of Ghasmarī is a snake, and in her left hand a yogic bowl.
To the right of Pukkasī is a lion, and likewise an axe in her left.
In the right [hand] of Śavarī is a mendicant’s bowl, and likewise a *khiṅkhirikā* in the left.
(32) In the right of Caṇḍālī is a discus, and likewise a plough in the left.
In the right of Ḍombī is a vajra, and likewise the right index finger raised in the left. (33)
Gaurī and the others are considered to have two arms, standing in the *ardhaparyaṅka* dance posture;
they are three-eyed, with hair standing erect, and adorned with the five mudrās.
Gaurī is black in color, and Caurī is like the sun in brilliance. (34)
Vetālī has the luster of molten gold; Ghasmarī resembles an emerald. (35) Pukkasī has the luster of an Indra-nīla sapphire; Śavarī has the radiance of a moonstone.
Caṇḍālī is dark blue like the sky; Ḍombī is considered to be the color of karcūra. (36)
Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, Rudra, Vaivasvata, Vināyaka, Nairṛti, and Vemacitrin [are the lords] of Gaurī and the others; their seats are [to be offered].
Having adorned the *bolaka* and having worshiped the Blessed One with devotion, (37) [one should proceed].
Nairātmyā asks for the mantra with firm embraces and kisses:
(38) "The mantra that brings women under control, as well as the one for threatening the wicked."

I shall now proclaim this mantra, which causes the hurling of the *nāgas* and crushes the gods and asuras; listen to it, O Goddess, bestower of happiness. It has been taught by me nowhere else than among the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. (39–40)
O Goddess, whatever has been done by Vajrasattva regarding this mantra, we are extremely afraid; it is spoken out of deference to you.
Having drawn the mandala, which is formidable with garlands of flames...
In order to bestow the consecration upon Vajragarbha, Tilottamā was drawn forth.
(42) By one who has performed ten thousand recitations clearly, with a long and beautiful sound, and who is joined in the yoga of Hevajra, all women are drawn forth. (43)
By reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, he whose self is yoga performs all activities through the vajra-yoga of the syllable *he*, with a mind free from fear.
Furthermore, [one should contemplate] the first of the Vedas, adorned with the half-moon and the bindu.
Afterwards, [one should worship] him who has eight faces, whose hair and eyebrows are tawny and upright;
then [him] who has twenty-four eyes, sixteen arms, a body like a dark cloud, and who wears many garlands of skulls.

To the one whose mind is exceedingly cruel toward the end, who has fangs like a crescent moon: (46) Slay! Slay! Cause to slay! Cause to slay! Roar! Roar! Threaten! Threaten! Dry up! Dry up the seven oceans! Bind! Bind the eight Nāgas! Seize! Seize the enemies! Ha hā hi hī hu hū he hai ho hau haṃ haḥ phaṭ svāhā! (47)
Then, satisfied by the practice of churning with the churning-stick, that goddess asked for a beautiful mandala through intense embraces and kisses.
There, the Teacher, possessed of great wisdom, himself drew the mandala.
With a joyful mind, composed through the union of the vajra and the lotus,
[one should visualize] a single enclosure with four gates, filled with various rays of light,
provided with four archways, and adorned with vajra-lines. (49–50)
One should then draw eight vases joined with five lines,
using powders made of the five precious gems, or else with rice and so forth,
or even with bricks from cremation grounds and likewise with charcoal from cremation grounds. (51)
In the center of that, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with filaments;
and in its pericarp, one should draw the deity Naraka, white in color and three-parted.
(52) Furthermore, one should draw Śarabha in the northeast and a mendicant in the southeast corner.
One should draw a wheel in the southwest and a vajra in the northwest;
likewise, one should draw a knife at the eastern gate and a fire-drill in the south.
In the west, one should draw a tortoise, and likewise a serpent in the north.
(54) The eight symbols are proclaimed according to the color-distinctions of the goddesses; in the center, one should draw a white skull-cup marked with a double-vajra. (55)
Then one should present the victory vase (*vijayakalaśa*), which has young sprouts at its opening, is wrapped in fine cloth, contains five gems within, is divine, and is filled with *śāli* rice.
(56) The mandala ritual should be performed just as it is in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*. (57)
And one should enter the maṇḍala with the eight great blissful vidyās, aged twelve or twice eight, adorned with necklaces and anklets:
the mother, the sister, the daughter, and the niece. (58)
Likewise, the wife of the maternal uncle, the mother’s sister, and the husband’s sister, as well as the father’s sister—these eight types are proclaimed.
The yogi should worship them with firm embraces and kisses. (59)
There, one should drink camphor; with that, the mandala is sprinkled. (60) The yogin should cause them to drink it, and he shall quickly attain accomplishment.
There, madana should be drunk, and one should eat balashalija. (61)
Having stripped her of her clothes, one should kiss her vulva again and again.
By means of them, the *bola* is stimulated; they sing and dance most excellently.
And there, play is performed through the union of the *bola* and the *kakkola*.
Afterwards, during the second watch, one should cause the disciple to enter there.
Having covered his eyes with a cloth, the mandala is shown to him;
there, at midnight in a secluded house, the consecration is bestowed. (63–64)
Just as the consecrations have been described according to the distinctions of the *ācārya* and so forth,
and just as the praise and worship were previously explained, they should be inferred by well-trained disciples.
And therein he should teach the reality (*tattva*) beginning with the *virama* and ending with the *parama*.
That which was hidden in all tantras has been revealed from its very depths.
Thereupon, that goddess asked through the practice of vajra-worship:
"O Lord, O Great Master, tell me: what is that moment like? (66–67)
The Blessed One said:
"Neither beginning nor end, nor middle; there is neither existence nor nirvana there."
This is that supreme great bliss;
it is neither other nor the self.
(68) As for the ring finger and the middle finger of one's own right hand...
The yogi should press those two together during sexual union; from that, the dual wave arises.
Afterwards, knowledge is born, like the pleasure of a maiden’s first experience. Something indescribable arises therein for the fool, like a dream.
The supreme end, the middle of the cessation, the empty and non-empty Heruka—
this is the fifth chapter, the *Hevajrābhyudaya*.
Part II. Chapter VI.
Having firmly embraced the goddess, having cast the *bola* into the skull-cup, having firmly grasped her breasts, and having smelled the human nose, (1)
Pressing the lips together with the tongue, making a scratch on the armpit with the nails,
and attaining bliss through the *saṃpuṭa* [mudrā], one manifests the five mudrās.
A ring is worn for the purpose of bowing to the Guru, the Ācārya, and the chosen deity.
To avoid hearing ill-spoken words, one should wear the earrings of Vajradhara upon the ears; a necklace for reciting mantras;
a breast-ornament to abandon the binding of living beings; and a girdle to cultivate the mudrās.
The body is always sealed by the seal of the five Buddhas.
(4) Then, having let out a loud laugh and biting her lower lip with her teeth, that goddess questioned Hevajra, who possesses the form of the Innate. (5)
"By what procedure and by what ritual action, O Lord, should the cloth painting (*paṭa*) of Hevajra be made? Tell me, O Great Bliss.
The Blessed One said:
Here, the practitioner who is a holder of the pledge, being himself a holder of the pledge, must paint the formidable cloth with five-colored pigments;
the Guru’s cloth should be painted using a brush made of human hair and a corpse’s hair. (7)

By that practitioner of the pledge (*samayinī*) who must perform the rite with the *sūtra* and that which must be performed with the cloth, through the yoga of the empowerment of the pledge (*samayādhiṣṭhāna*),
on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of every month in a secluded house—
At midday, with a cruel mind and somewhat intoxicated by wine,
having become naked upon his body and thus being utterly bare,
he should then consume the pledge-substance that has been cast off and rendered impure. (9–10)

Having placed his own consort to his left—she who has a beautiful face, is compassionate, possesses beauty, youth, and charm, is adorned with fine flowers, and is dear to the practitioner. The sixth chapter: The Procedure for the Hevajra Cloth-Painting.
Part II, Chapter VII.
Then, in that place, that goddess spoke by means of the union of the *bola* and *kakkola*:
Pressing the lip with the tooth, how does the book come to be? Through the union of the vajra and the lotus, the delighted deity manifests. (1) The Blessed One said:
Listen, O highly fortunate goddess, I shall describe the book:
one who has taken the vow should write a twelve-finger-length book upon birch bark.
Having made ink from great honey with a pen made of human bone,
if a mouse should see either the book or the cloth painting,
there will be no accomplishment in this life, nor within the sphere of the next world.
The vision of that which is employed through the oral tradition must at times be concealed;
the book [should be hidden] in the hair, in the armpit, or on the path.
Having placed the *liṅga* in the *bhaga* and having kissed it again and again...
Having fully accomplished great bliss, the Vajra-holder should prescribe the meal.
Listen, O large-eyed Goddess, to the meal in the maṇḍala of the assembly;
when it is consumed, there arises the accomplishment that fulfills all desires and aims. (5–6)
In a cremation ground, in a mountain thicket, or likewise in a city of non-humans, or else in a solitary border region, one should begin this meal.
There, one should fashion a seat called the "New," having the form of a corpse. (7)
Alternatively, [one should place] a tiger skin and likewise a cloth from a cremation ground.

Then, having assumed the form of Hevajra in the center, one should assign the yoginīs to their respective positions according to the previous method, in the cardinal and intermediate directions. (8–9)
One should eat upon a tiger skin, using *mālatī* wood as fuel for the ritual commitment (*samaya*).
There, one should diligently consume *rājaśāli* rice as food.
Having eaten again and again there, the Mothers are worshipped. (10)
Or if one should worship intensely one's mother, sister, niece, or sister-in-law, they will attain accomplishment in the maṇḍala of the Gaṇas.
(11) A single piece of divine great hell, filled with passion—
The fortunate one should give it to the Guru and drink it himself after having paid homage.
He should receive it with the lotus-hand and give it back with that very same hand;
meanwhile, the practitioner performs prostrations there again and again. (12–13)
The seventh chapter: On Food.
Part II, Chapter VIII. There, the yoginīs ask: "O giver of bliss, tell us what Mahāmudrā is like in its conventional form. (1)
The Blessed One said:
"Neither too long nor too short, neither black nor pale."
Her breath has the appearance and color of a lotus petal and is fragrant;
her sweat is likewise fragrant, possessing a luster like that of musk.
She exudes the scent of the lotus and the blue water-lily, acting like a black lotus.
A wise person should perceive her fragrance as being like camphor and *sihlaka*;
her scent may also be like that of a blue lotus or similar to black agallochum.
She is steadfast, unwavering, speaks kindly, and is enchanting.
One with beautiful hair and a waist marked by three folds is considered a natural *padminī*;
having attained her, there arises the perfection (*siddhi*) whose nature is innate bliss.
(5) Then the Yoginī Nairātmyā said:
"Blessed One, what kind of vow should be made?
The Blessed One replied:
"One born of noble family, free from madness, observing the commitments (samaya), and a teacher of Hevajra."
May I be compassionate and devoted to my guru in birth after birth.
(6) With hands ringing the vajra and bell, may I be a reciter of the profound Dharma;
may I partake of the semen of women in birth after birth. (7)
Thereupon, that goddess, being pleased, spoke these words:
"By what means indeed are beings who are difficult to tame and difficult to subdue brought to discipline?
The Blessed One said:
First the Poṣadha is given, and after that the ten precepts;
there one should teach the Vaibhāṣya and likewise the Sūtrānta. After that, the Yogācāra, and following that, one should teach the Madhyamaka. (9)
Having understood the entire system of mantras, one should thereafter undertake Hevajra.
The disciple should receive it with reverence; he will attain accomplishment—of this there is no doubt. (10) The eighth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Those to be Disciplined."
Part II. Chapter IX.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the *saṃpuṭa* and *udghāta*, by the mere knowledge of which the practitioner shall attain accomplishment (*siddhi*).
The practitioner, with a cruel internal mind, should uproot [the victim] at the navel of the one to be accomplished by means of his hand, visualizing himself in the form of Heruka;
by mere meditation alone, even a Buddha will certainly perish. (1–2)
Killing is performed out of compassion after having informed the Guru, the Sage;
[it is directed at] one who acts with hostility toward the Teaching and is a destroyer of the Guru and the Buddha.
Having seen such a person in their true form, one should visualize them with their face turned downward.
And [one should meditate on him] vomiting blood, shaking with his hair standing on end;
one should visualize a needle, having the form of fire, entering into his path.
Having visualized the seed-syllable of fire in the heart, one may cause death at that very moment.
(5) In this tantra, there is no need for fire-offerings nor for the performance of mudrā-bindings;
this great tantra is accomplished through recitation alone and is mastered by mere meditation. (6)
I shall speak the supreme secret; listen, O Goddess of beautiful countenance!
It is the delightful purification of existence, which bestows the accomplishment free from conceptual construction.
Behold, O Goddess, the great jewel, a body enveloped in garlands of flames.
That which is unpierced is useless, but once pierced, it bestows radiance.
(8) In the same way, the jewel of cyclic existence, though endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure, becomes poison when impure, but becomes like nectar when purified. (9)
I shall speak of the form in which that Lord arose—the Heruka-form who delivers the world from saṃsāra—for those who listen.
His eyes are red with compassion, and his body is black due to his mind of loving-kindness. (10)
The four feet are said to be the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).

(11) In this [form], there are eight faces, eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), and sixteen arms; by the seal (*mudrā*), there are the five Buddhas, and he is wrathful for the sake of disciplining the wicked. (12)
Pukkasi is known by means of flesh; Śavarī is conceived through blood;
Caṇḍālī is said to be semen; and Ḍombī is [the essence] of fat and marrow. Skin is the seven factors of enlightenment, while bone is the four truths. (13)
The Goddess said:
"O Mahāsukha, tell me what the extraction of the mantra (*mantroddhāra*) should be like, by which mantra the actions of living beings attain perfection. (14)
The Blessed One, the Great Vajra-holder, whose body is the essence of the vajra, said:
"Listen, O Goddess of great fortune; I shall tell you the mantra.
First, having placed Vairocana, [followed by] the fourth of the sibilants..."
One should employ the divine Pukkasi-mantra, beautiful, white in color, and surmounted by the syllable of emptiness (ŚŪ), ending with SVĀHĀ.
By reciting this one hundred thousand times, one shall always paralyze the world. (16)
Having first given the Lord of Letters, then the Sky-walker (Khecari),
and having joined it with "svāhā" at the end, one may bring even the Buddhas under one's control.
Having given the first of the Vedas, [one should give] the second of the first.
One should employ the mantra ending in *śūnya* and *svāhā*; it can even cause the Buddhas to be expelled.
Having first placed Vairocana, one takes the third letter of the second [vowel], conjoined with *ra* and adorned with *va*, followed by *śūnya* and joined at the end with *svāhā*.
One should cause all humans to hate [the enemy].
First, having placed the Lord of Letters (*varṇeśvara*), one takes the third letter of the fifth [vowel-group].
Accompanied by the syllable *śūnya* and joined with *ḍākinī*, ending in *svāhā*, it is for malevolent rites (*abhicāruka*).
Having again bestowed the eldest of the letters, resembling a red *hūṃ* and ending in *svāhā*, one may instantly summon Rambhā and others, including Tilottamā. (20–21)
First, having uttered the *mohakula* mantra, one should employ the syllable *ghu*;
then, having again appended *svāhā*, one may slay gods and humans.
Of the first [mantra], the first is joined with the *vajraḍākinī*.
Having first placed Vairocana, [one places] the second of the semivowels;
joined with Vajraḍākinī, [one places] the foremost of the first [group].
Joined with Vajraḍākinī, [one places] the third of the semivowels. (23–24)
Again, joined with that very same [syllable], and adorned above by *caurī*, one should apply the syllable *hrīḥ* there; one should perform it again, ending with *svāhā*.
This is the mantra of Kurukullā. (25)
The third letter of the fourth [varga] beginning with *oṃ*, adorned by Caurī;
the fourth of the semivowels (*antasthā*), joined with Picu-vajra;
and the fourth of the sibilants (*ūṣman*), adorned by Pukkasī. (26)
The second letter of the fifth [varga], tripled and conjoined with the void (śūnya).
The first [mantra] of the third [section], ending with *svāhā*, is the heart-mantra of Hevajra,
joined with *vairocanādijvalajvalaya*.
The fourth of the fifth [group], joined with the first of the semivowels and adorned by Ghasmarī;
and the fourth of the sibilants, adorned by Vajraḍākinī. (28)
The syllable ŚŪṂ, followed by the second letter of the fifth [varga] tripled,
then the first letter of the third [varga], ending with SVĀHĀ— this is the mantra of the Four-Armed One. (29)
The first [mandala] of Vairocana and the others is adorned with Gaurī in the inner circle;
the first [mandala] of the third is likewise adorned with Gaurī in the inner circle. (30)

Having doubled the third of the fifth [vowel] and the third of the second [consonant], adorned with fire (*ra*) and joined with three *hūṃ* syllables; the second of the fifth [vowel] and the first of the third [consonant], ending with *svāhā*, is the mantra of the Six-Armed One. (31) The first of the fourth [vowel] starting from Vairocana, conjoined with fire (*ra*) and adorned with Vetālī; the third of the semivowels (*antasthā*), adorned with Ghasmarī; the first of the first [consonants], joined with the first of the semivowels and adorned with a vajra. (32)

The syllable *kṣa*, adorned by Caurī; the first of the fifth [group], the fourth of the sibilants (*uṣman*), adorned by Vajraḍākinī, and surmounted by the Void (*śūnya*); tripled; ending with *phaṭ svāhā*. This is for the two-armed [Heruka].

(33) The first of the first, the first of the second, the first of the third, the first of the fourth, the first of the fifth, the first of the semivowels (*antaḥsthāna*), and the first of the sibilants (*uṣman*); ending with *svāhā* preceded by Vairocana and the others. This is the mantra for agitating the city, to be recited one hundred thousand times. (34)

The second of the semivowels (*antasthā*), namely the two *kṣa* syllables; again, in the middle, the second of the semivowels; three *hūṃ* syllables interspersed with *phaṭ* syllables, ending with *svāhā*. This is the mantra for purifying the ground.
(35) Following that, Vairocana and the others, ending with *vajra hūṃ*, is the mantra for the consecration of food and drink. (36)

Following Vairocana and the others, the letter *A* is the mouth; the third of the sibilants (*Ṣ*); the fourth of the semivowels (*V*) adorned above with fire (*R*). This is for the phenomena (*dharmāṇām*). Following that, because they are primordially unarisen, there is *VAJRA*. Thus, *Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā* is the mantra for the bali offering to all elemental spirits (*sarvabhautika*).
The ninth chapter, on the extraction of mantras.
Part II. Chapter X.
Now, therefore, he who is called Vajrasattva, the single vow of all phenomena, having kissed Nairātmyā, reveals the sphere of recitation. (1)
Stambhana is performed with crystal; for vaśya, red sandalwood is used;
abhicāruka with riṣṭika stone; likewise, vidveṣa with boneless [substances];
uccāṭana with horse-hoof; and ākarṣaṇa with the bone of a Brahmin.

Rain is brought by means of elephant bones; the killing of an enemy is achieved with the [bones] of a buffalo. For paralyzing, one should drink milk; for subjugation, one may act according to one's own will.
For killing, one uses *sihlaka* (stickleback resin), and for attraction, the "four-fold equal" (*catuḥsama*) compound.
For causing enmity, rice is prescribed; for eradication, musk.
Alternatively, [the mantras] beginning with *antaśva*, *ādiśva*, *nādi*, *gādi*, and likewise *hādi* [are used].
(5) This is the tenth chapter, named the Chapter on Recitation (*jāpa*).
Part II, Chapter XI.
Embracing Hevajra firmly and pressing his lower lip with her teeth, Nairātmyā asks him there concerning the family forms of embodied beings. (1)
"Having established the *liṅga* in the *bhaga*, so says the Lord of the Wheel.
I shall describe the own family (*svakula*) of embodied beings; listen, O Prajñāpāramitā! (2)
If at the base of the ring finger there should be a nine-pronged vajra for either a woman or a man, that is the supreme Akṣobhya family.
There shall be a wheel for Vairocana, and a lotus for Amitābha.

Ratnasaṃbhava is the great jewel, and Khaḍga is that of the Karma family. (4) For whichever yogin is black, Akṣobhya is his deity; for whichever yogin is very white, Vairocana is the deity of his family. (5)
For the yogin who is dark blue, his deity is Amoghasiddhi;
for the yogin who is deep orange, his family deity is Ratneśa.
Indeed, for the yogin who is reddish-white, his family deity is Amitābha.
For that yogin who is white and fair, the family of Vajrasattva shall arise.
(7) Living beings should not be held in contempt nor harmed by those who have reached the further shore of yoga;
they belong to the families of the Tathāgatas, having resorted to conventional form. (8)
The characteristics of women are exactly like those of men;
their families likewise exist according to their concealment, conduct, and appearance.
Therein, the Great Vajrin was pleased by the kissing of the female and male organs.
He awakened [her] to selflessness; listen, O Goddess, to the method of worship.
(10) In a garden, in a secluded place, or within one’s own quarters, the knower of yoga should always worship the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) after having stripped her naked. (11)

Having performed kissing and embracing, as well as touching the vulva, [the yogin] always performs the act with the hands of the limbs of passion upon the testicles and the drinking of the honey of the lower lip from the human nose.
(12) Bolavān always performs this work with the hands that are the limbs of *madana*.

With the elbow of the swinging limb likewise well-extended, the wielder of the vajra should desire [union] again and again; he should gaze downward and upward. He attains vast accomplishment and becomes equal to all Buddhas.
There, camphor is consumed, and especially madana;
one should partake of strength there for the sake of camphor.
(15) Part II, Chapter XII.
This is a section entitled "The Chapter on the Meaning of the Innate."
Then, therefore, the Vajra-holder spoke of the four empowerments:
"Taking the great vajra and the great bell, established in the vajra, perform this very day the gathering of disciples for the Vajra-ācārya. (1)
Just as the sons of enlightenment were sprinkled by the Buddhas of the past,
so have you been sprinkled by me with the secret consecration through the stream of mind. (2)
"Seize, seize the Goddess who bestows delight, who bestows accomplishment, who possesses universal form, and who is enchanting! Having seized her, O Great Being, perform worship!
This knowledge is exceedingly subtle, the vajra-mandala, comparable to space."
Stainless, bestowing liberation, and peaceful—you yourself are your own father.
(4) This is the mantra for the empowerment of the vajra-lotus.
Oṃ! O Lotus, support of bliss, bestower of the bliss of great passion!
O you whose nature is the four joys, Viśva! Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ! Accomplish my purpose! (5) Oṃ! O Vajra, great hatred, bestower of the four joys!
O Lord, whose single flavor is the mouth of the bird, perform my task: *hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ*.
Place the syllable *oṃ* on the head, the syllable *hūṃ* at the heart, and the syllable *āḥ* in the filaments.
The second chapter of the *Māyākalpa*, the Great King of Tantras.
